div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DZAIi NELLIE, Although they are sadly unserviceable, the gowns of the season are quite exceptionally pretty. Muslins are of many types, and some new variety seems to appear every day. There are the organdis soft of texture and daintily flowered: embroidered white and ecru muslins; hair-cord muslins with graceful patterns straying over the cords, and self-coloured muslins, especially in deep shades of blue, mauve, and cerise. The universal - trimming is lace, generally in the form of waved insertions laid on the material. Besides the muslins there are some charming novelities in silk. zephyrs and printed cottons, which really make up nearly as smartly as the more costly silks. Foulard will be greatly wore this year, and the very newest kind is dotted over with mingled ‘. black and white spots on a cherry-red or blue ground. This makes up excellently with a gathered skirt trimmed with three rows of waved lace insertion and a bodice striped with the same and cut open in a point at the throat to show a little lace vest, which may be lined or, if for real hot-weather wear, left transparent.

Present appearances show that there will soon be nothing smarter than poppy-coloured crêpe, especially for great occasions, when a crepe de Chine skirt with a brocade coat will be the latest and most desirable fashian there can be. Poppy hats and toques are in demand, and those who want to show that the fashion has not come theft way in vain can have poppy cravats or a bunch oi the flowers in their rustic straw hats. Needles to say, black velvet goes exceedingly well with these scarlet flowers. Black mercury wings in a poppy red toque make a good choice for morning wear. For more dressy occasions there is a dis• position to favour biscuit-coloured straw, trimmed with masses of tea roses and glossy green leaves.

to really seems as if, as each season comes round, we hear of the anticipated demise of the blouse, but in spite of all predictions the blouse, like cracked china, lives long. This summer it bids fair to be more popular than ever, and the most chic will be the muslin slips with insertions of lace. White, or very pale shades of cashmere, are being employed for blouses, the fineness of modern cashmere making it a most acceptable substance for blouses. White and black tulle bows, big and outstanding, are much worn at present as a reliev- ing touch at the throat, but plenty of material, quite two to two and a-half yards, is required, or they will look skimpy or inefficient to begin with. The white tulle is a welcome intervention between the all-black toilette, and the face, for dead, un- relieved black is very seldom becoming to any complexion, especially to those no longer in their youth.

Simplicity 'l's what fashion demands. It is a simplicity difficult to achieve, becausn there must be distinction with it, an ieffect on the very cierier can produce. • Two methods of securing it are by using lace bands and tucks in company in a cloth out-of-door dress. The lace is of a bold character, and forms a simulated tunic or a band running right round the skirt, while on the bodice naturally the bolero provides a good motif, and on the sleeves the bands run round the arm, the besi method of securing the flatness necessary to the display of a strikingly-patterned lace.

‘. A short bolero, in every sort of aerial and of every. description, IS a safe purchase. The smart world shows no sign of tiring of theni yet awhile, and wears them on every available occasion. Some are very pretty, meeting a shaped belt of embroidery which still keeps the lengthening effect of the waist.
Your loving JENNIES.

div.head: CUAPTER XXXI.
div.p: CUAPTER XXXI.

Stephen Hart lay in the military hospital at Pietermaritzburg. The wound he had received on the Elands Laagte battlefield still pained him greatly, as the bullet, located near the right shoulder-blade, had not yet been extracted. Being a dum-dum missile, also, it had inflicted serious injury after entering his body, and whilst the surgeons had counteracted its bad effects somewhat, yet the fact that it remained embedded where it had first lodged threatened disaster to the patient.

Many attempts were made to dislodge it, but without avail. At last Steve, losing heart as his condition became daily worse, ceased to hope that he would .be restored to health and strength again. He assured himself that he had nothing to live for, nothing to hope for. Why did he not jump into the Capetown dock, twelve months ago, and drown himself as he had intended to do ? Then there; would have been an end of his miserable life. What use had this extra year of existencitbeen to him ? True! he had made the acquaintance of the kindly Barnard, but—he had already lost him. He had been enabled to render a slight service to his Queen and country, but now even this thought failed to give him any. gratification. Life was dreary, weary, hopeless. He would be glad when his turn came to leave it. He prayed that it would be soon. He would welcome death gladly. Day by day he saw the curtains pulled round the beds about him, and knew that a comrade had answered the last roll-call. Ah, how he envied these poor fellows ! No torturing, racking pain was theirs, no agonising, distracting thoughts. When the Salvation Army captain had spoken of good Sister Ella, Steve, for a time, associated the kindly Sister with a certain Ella Rayburn he had known of old. Perhaps this gentle spirit, this ministering angel, was his Ella—yeincarnated • per- haps she had passed through the refining fire of tri- bulation and suffering' and emerged a new woman. He cherished this notion for a considerable time, and it gave him a new heart, and he was feverishly eager to encounter this rare spirit, be she his Ella or not.

Cartleigh, in his drunken declaration in the Johannesburg market-place, had said that she had flown from him. Without a doubt she had repented of her heartlessness. Though there were many Ellas, Fe felt convinced that this Sister Ella was none other than Ella Rayburn. But now as his strength failed, as his body writhed in agonising pain, his mind -viewed all things differently. Life was black, life was hell, a dreadful hell peopled with she-devils, of whom one, Ella Rayburn, was queen. Bah HoW could.- he ever conceive that that abandoned creature could ever be capable of repentance? . How could he ever imagine that she, the heartless hussy who had indited • that black epistle to him, could ever be transformed into an angel of love and light? Banish the thought! He must have been mad to cherish it, even for a second! _ _ , _

rn his paroxysms of pain and anguish the tortured trooper bit viciously the sheet that covered him. Blood marked the white coverlet, and an attendant passing near, perceiving it, came to speak soothing words to the sufferer.
"Ah, poor fellow, the pain is more than you can bear !" _ _

"It's not the bodily pain; I can bear that, but 0 God! it's the pain here." He touched his head with his left Ilmd. "It's here. lam going mad, I think! Put an end to me! For pity's sake, do!" From his fevered brow the sweat drops coursed down his drawn cheeks.
"Let there be an end of it! Let me die. I don't want to live! "
The man at his side wiped his moist brow tenderly. -

"Oh, pluck up, my lad. We'll soon have you right. You're weak and feverish. It's that cursed Boer bullet that's troubling you. It's out of its element. It's foreign stuff, and nothing 'foreign should be in you; you're British to the backbone, lad, and being British, you'll pull through." The patient groaned wearily. The attendant continued, cheerily: "We'll soon have you right, my lad. We've a rattling English surgeon coming to-morrow, a great fellow he is, Sir William something. A tip-topper he is, the fellows say. Draws bullets from their billets as easily as a dentist extracts your molars, and with less pain. Wait till he gets hold of you, my lad. He'll soon send that bothering bullet back to Pretoria, and send you home to England smiling and gay. Despite himself, Steve was compelled to smile at the fellow's raillery. . "The only thing that we're concerned about is this: We think that the new surgeon may go the way of some of the others' and get mashed on the special nurses who are looking after the con- dalescents. A spanking lot of girls they are, my lad, especially one of 'em; one look from her will cure a fellow of all his sickness—but love-sickness; she gives him that awful bad. I half envy you the opportunities you'll have of seeing the nursing staff, and .being nursed by them. Perhaps the special one .will attend you. If so, be ready to go to the front again in less than a week. But whatever you do don't fall in love with the girl or —marry her." The chatty attendant departed, and presently Steve fell into a troubled sleep. On the morrow he was conveyed to the operating- room, and there saw the eminent surgeon of whom the attendant had spoken. Antesthetics were quickly applied, and when Steve again woke to consciousness, he looked round on a strange place, a spacious, lofty, cool, and well-ventilated chamber, far different to the one he had previously occupied. Ranged round the room were rows of cots on which soldier comrades reclined. The building was a puzzle to Steve. It was not a 'church, nor a school, nor a barracks; nor was it a sanitorium or a hospital, though now used for hospital purposes. "It's the Town Hall, mate," said a Manchester man, in the next cot, answering his query. "Yes, it's the 'Maritzburg Town Hall, and we are the common councillors. You haven't seen it before ? " "No," answered Steve. "The last place I remember being in was the operating-room.' "The butcher's shop, eh? I know. We've all been there. Nice place to spend a Christmas holiday in, eh? I went in with two arms and two legs. Came out with one leg and three-quarters, and this I " He raised the stump of his right arm. "The other's gone altogether. Must have kept it for a keepsake; the arms that Tommy's left behind him.' This is what comes of being 'men at arms.' The arms an' legs 'at Tommy's left behind him, will be another subjeck •for a pome by Mr. Kipling. Eh? Oh, you don't know him, of course. You've been sort of out of the world lately." "I have," said Steve. "I felt out of the world entirely, shut up in that dull hospital." "Yes, I know. I've been there, too. But here were all right; this is a gay place. We live like Members of Parliament and fighting cocks here—l mean so far as the grub and the style goes. And we've got beautiful girls to _nurse us, too, though I'm a married man, worse luck I Let's see, what was I saying? Oh, about Kipling. He's a poet- chap, you know; slings verses and that sort of thing, and I tell you he does it prime. He knows Tommy, if any man does. Well, this Kipling has written some poetry about us chaps, and it's prime, ray boy, prime! Fits us 'dbwn to the ground. !And it's fairly knocked the folks at home, and theY're giving their thousands and thousands, and —well, .I°4 here, mate, this money that's being given to the 'Absent-minded beggars' is coming in mighty handy. When we Manchesters, with you tight Horse chaps, and the Gordons and the Devnns,' made that last rush, my last thought was of Molly and the kids, but I know now that they're all right, and have had their bit of plum-pudding this Christmas," "Christmas!" exclaimed Steve. "What! Is it Christmas? " "Not Christmas now, chummy, but it was a few days ago." • "I must have been bad a long time, then. I thought we were only at the beginning of December yet." "Not the beginning, but the end. You have been Rip Van Winkling, mate, and no mistake. I heard one of the nurses say that you had been uncon- scious, off and on, for weeks. You'd swallowed a bullet, and it wouldn't digest, I heard. But you feel better now, elm? " "I feel all right now," said Steve, as really he did. "But you're not all right by a long chalk yet, chummy. We all feel like that when we've got an indigeitible load off tho stomach. But. you're not

div.head: CHAPTER XXXII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXXII.

The nurse, prim and clean in her becoming dress and cap, came up to the two men and intently regarded Steve. "You must not talk so much yet," she said: "though I'm glad to see that you have regaineu speech and consciousness again."

- "Wouldn't Nurse Ella- wake a stone to con- sciousness and make it speak ? " observed the Man- chester warrior, drily. "I really believe she would," the nurse answered, with a smile. "She has certainly exercised her hypnotic influence on our friend here and brought him round when others failed. She sat with you for hours last night," she said, turning to Steve. "Yes, hs-ars ! Think of itl "said the Manchester man. "flours, my boy, she sat with you, Nurse Ella did„ when some of our chaps would have revelled in minutes, or even seconds. You must think yourself mightily honoured, my. lad, to be attended for hours by Nurse Ella." "Ile appreciates the honour, I am sure," said Nurse Marian.

"I am deeply 'grateful to Nurse Ella for her great kindness," satd Steve, speaking somewhat stiffly, though striving to refrain from so doing. "Deeply grateful? 'said his neighbour patient. "Deeply grateful, man! Why, if I'd been .you nursed for hours by Nurse Ella I'd have trotted out all the adjectives and nomnitives, and subjictives, and other parts of speech ,and grammar, and I'd have rolled them into one magnificent, over- whelming, graitudinous sentence, the like of which was never seen—or heard before; And I wouldn't have stopped at sPeech, parts of speech, or any other sort either. I'd have acted; I'd have kissed, kissed, and blessed; and hugged, and gone on my knees to—that is if I'd had two whole legs—have gone on my knees to Nurse Ella, and offered her my eternal, and diurnal, and supernal gratitude. That's what I'd have done . . . No, purse, don't stop me yet, it's only my fun. It'll cheer chummy here up. It'll be good physic for him so long as Nurse Ella isn't here to completely cure him with her smiles. I only want him to know that he's the most honoured man in this Town Hall, and that's saying a lot, for I see yonder is Sir Billy himself. Our chummy is, I say, the most honoured man in the show, for though he's not been here many hours Nurse Ella seems to take a bigger interest in him than in anybody else. I know. I'm not always sleeping when I've my eyes shut, and I sqw her last night. Yes, I know what I know; and though I'm not, going to split on our Miss Heat.all, I say that if prayers will cure any- body' hers will cure .chummy, here." That night,Stephen Hart lapsed for a short period into a feverish state again. Nurse-Ella- sat`by his side administering the medicine prescribed for the rambling patient. When calm, restful sleep super- vened she still kept her vigil, gazing "lovingly on the pale face before her. Once for a moment she slipped to her knees, and, had the Manchester man in the adjoining cot then been observing her, he would have plainly heard her fervent prayer. At midnight the large hall was in semi-darkness, and an air of peace was over all. Most of the patients were asleep. One only at the far corner of the room conversed in a low, subdued voice with Nurse Marian.

Ella Rayburn, weary with much, longTwatching,, day and night, at the bedsides of wounded soldiers, fell forward at last, and her head 'rested on the pillow before her. Nurse Marian, perceiving her, remarked to her companion: "Poor girl ! Let her sleep, she is completely worn out. Her whole thought has been of that poor Light Horse man ever since he was brought in here yesterday. Let her sleep, dear soul, and may she sleep soundly." Stephen Hart woke from sleep with a start. He had been dreaming of the Elands Laagte battle. Again had gone through that night Of horror, again had dashed forward with his gleaming blade, again had, heard the shouts, the curses, the screams, the piercing prayers for mercy. And as the babel of terrible sounds, the shouts, the clang of weapons, the roar ot guns, the rattle of musketry burst on his ear he awoke to find himself in a haven of peace, lying in a clean, comfortable cot, with a guardian angel at his side. Surely she must be an angel, this kindly nurse, who had tended him and others so lovingly. He would like to see her face. But 'here the light was dim, and her hair had fallen forward and partly obscured her features. Gently he stroked the brown tresses aside; the nurse moved in her sleep and her face came more into view. He bent towards her and peered anxiously, tremblingly into her visage.

"Good God !It is she! Ella! Ella!" he gasped, involuntarily. She awoke with a stifled cry, a cry of pain, yet a cry of rejoicing. "Steve!" she cried, aloud, and her arms were about him, and she sobbed on his bosom. The Manchester man, roused suddenly from slumber, blinked wonderingly, then, taking in the situation at a glance, turned over with his back to the whispering twain. "Knew how it would turn out," he grunted. "Bound to be a love affair and yum-yum business after the way she's fussed over him. And, hang it! He's only doing just what I told him he ought to do, kissing and hugging her for all he's worth.• Well, good luck to 'em I'm going to sleep again."

div.head: CHAPTER XXXIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXXIII.

For a full hour the Light Horse trooper and Nurse Ella whispered together animatedly. The man in the adjoining cot was at length aroused by their more audible speech, and, simulating sleep, he snored loudly to warn the lovers of his near proximity. But unheeding they conversed on.

"Yes,; said Nurse Ella, "the Salvation Army, that much-abtAed body of people, gave me timely shelter and protection in Johannesburg, and I was deeply grateful to them for it. Their religion did not consist in mere public preaching and street- corner shouting, they did much quiet, useful work. I helped to do a little of it. How, I need not say.' "I can well guess," said Steve. "You began the kindly, self-sacrificing work then which ultimately brought you here." "I have tried to do my best for others, Steve, this last twelve months," said Nurse Ella. "I have endeavoured to expiate my past folly and selfishness. Oh, when I come to look back on my old selfish, wilful, foolish life, I wonder that ever I was permitted to live! I have been a vain, shallow, thoughtless girl, Steve, and worse—wicked and cruel to you above all others. Oh, how I have suffered for my wrong-doing! But, Steve, I did not commit the greatest sin. Heaven was merciful, and saved me from that. I thought of you—ever of you, Steve; and, god helping me, I have been true to you." " "I believe you, my girl t" said the trooper, with trembling voice. "And you forgive me, Steve ? " "Forgive you? Yes; but it is I who need ask forgiveness of you. I have been a fool; I have wronged you. "You have been sorely tried."

"And you ? " "Yes; but, 0 Steve, I feel the better for it." "And I too, dearest." Then the Manchester man heard much kissing, 'and he writhed uneasily on his couch. ' "What Are they at it yet? Great Scott , When I went to sleep, two hours ago, they were yurn-yummin', and ducky-darling each other then! Seems to me that Light Horse chap is going to monopolise Nurse Ella altogether. He'll never have done with his `deeply grateful' work And to think that I put him up to it! Oh, laws !it is torture It's worse than a dum-dum bullet for knocking a fellow dumb ! " . , Daylight was now streaming through the im- provised hospital, and as the patients roused from slumber one by one, the nurses And attendants became busier. - - -

Ella Rayburn was leaving Steve's cot as the chief surgeon came to make his usual round of inspection. "Ah, my girl! I see," he said, in tones of mock reproof. "You are becoming too much attached to the British Army, or at least to certain fragmentary portions of it. I:shall have to report you.,, "For excessive zeal in the execution of her duty," added a junior surgeon, who had oft cast admiring and covetous eyes on the pretty nurse. "Exactly. For displaying excessive zeal in the execution of your duty, I shall report you, Nurse

. . 1,1„. "All 5414,, doctor," an9vraged Ella, smilingly. "Ind ifi-after you have reported me, I am dis- charged—Vshall get married at once!" '. , "Married!" Mohamed the surgeon, in dismay. . " Yes ; speak to Trooper ffart," said Ella, and bounded off, laughing gaily.

"Miss Rayburn:. I wish to speak to you a few moments," said the surgeon a few days later, as he drew the popular nurse into his private room. "Sit down, my girl, and make yourself as com- fortable as you can, for I am going to talk to you like a father."

Ella demurely obeyed, and the surgeon, having fixed his pince-nez in position on his eminent nose, clasped his hands under his eminent coat- tails, and regarded the blushing maiden with a quaint smile.
- "I am told that you are thinking about getting married, Miss Rayburn."
"Yes; sir."

"Ha Irm ! Well, that's all right, my girl, and only what one expects a pretty miss like you will do. But you mustn't think of getting married just yet." He met Ella's glance of amused inquiry. "No, not yet, my girl. The British Army can't spare you; her Majesty, our gracious Queen, can't spare you; I can't spare you, nor can my confreres or your fellow-nurses—not one of us can spare you yet." Ella essayed to speak, but he proceeded. _ _

"Had I known- that fellow- Hart would have desired,to take you off so soon, I believe I would have left that Boer memento in his ystern a little longer. You smile. Oh, but I'm seriouk A nice return this is for all our kindness to him 11 When we have cured him, he wants to run oft with Our best nurse."

"Oh, but—l've helped to cure him," said Ella, with a coquettish toss of her head.- " Ah, of course you have, my- girl. Our good surgery and your good nursing have accomplished it. But softly, Miss Rayburn. We'll keep him in the convalescent state yet a little while, then if he talks of getting up or getting married, I'll tell him that I shall send him to the front again." Ella gave a little start. "0 sir, you wouldn't think of doing that ! "

"No, ICion't think I would," he ari-swered, with a sly grin on his good-natured face. "We'll not send him to war again; he has done his duty well. We'll preserve him for the married state. But you mustn't get " married yet, my child. We really can't spare you. Wait till the war is over. Whatever should we do if you got married? Why, all the other nurses would want to follow your example, for everything that Nurse Ella does is right. You are the life and soul of the place, my girl; you have set a noble example to all in your devotion to this, the noblest work which man or woman can undertake. When the war is over, when the last batch of our unfortunate fellows have been dealt with, marry then, my girl, and I'll give you away myself. Only promise to remain with us a short time longer—say, until our troops enter Pretoria !"
"I'll gladly promise, said Ella, beaming radiantly.

"Ah, I knew you would, when I'd talked to you. It's that impatient fellow in the far cot whols so anxious to tie the connubial knot at once. Go, tell him he is a convalescent for thiree months longer yet! ,Soon after, he can get married; then, if you care lo settle in sunny Natal for a-time, I will fin,t,l him a good position." Warmly thanking the kindly surgeon, Ella returned to her duties, happy in the knowledge that she had lived to earn the esteem of such a man;' happy, too, to know that she had the regard of all her fellow-workers and the devotion of all the patients; happiest to know, and feel, and momen- tarily realise, that she had the whole-hearted love of Stephen , Hart, her -lover of old, her lover through all time. Happy Ella 1 As the weeks and months wore on and the cots about her continued to be filled .with fresh faces, one face still remained looking lovingly upon her as she flitted about, a true ministering angel. - -
S-teve had now well-nigh recovered, and, with other convalescents, was permitted to sit up in bed and peruse the papers recording the progress of the war and the continued success of British arms.
One night, after reading an account of a brilliant engagement, in which the enemy was totally routed, he fell back asleep.
An. Irishman, 'who now occupied the next cot, reached over, and gently drew the newspaper from the hands of the slumberer.

"Begorra I A wake man can be More enlightened than a sleepy one," he said, holding the paper before him; "arid sure, news of battle restin' on his chest, would give him bcl. drames. Let him slape soundly." But he did not sleep soundly, for presently Nurse Ella came in his vicinity, and he woke instantly; and when the Irishman slyly peeped round the edge of his paper, he perceived the trooper beckoning to the nurse. A moment later Pat was busily scanning the headlines of the "war news." " 'Continued Success of British Arms.' Yes,. begorra I "—as he cast a glance at his neighbour— "yes, look at his British arms successfully encir- cling her shapely waist! Good luck to British arms Success to 'em I"

_ Now, as the months wore on, _ the din of battle ceased, the war drums throbbed no longer, the bells which "t4,lled for the brave" became silent, and gave place to peace bells, joy bells, wedding bells. Steve the Outlander, an Outlander no more in the land across the Vaal, was united in wedlock with Ella Rayburn at Pretoria.
The surgeon gave the bride away, and Henry Cartleigh was the groom's "best maa." f TUE END..]

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

Much has been done by bazaars and entertainments in aid of the War Fandrethough it is clear that these efforts will not alone suffice to provide for the returning stream of disabled warriors. One of the most useful of charit- able institutions is Princess Christian'e Horne for dis- abled Soldiers arid Sailors, and it is hoped to realise a large sum for this good work at the forthcoming Royal Naval, and Military Bazaar at Olympia. on June 19, 20, and 21. At the same time, war is the country's affair, and the permacent maintenance of the men who can no longer earn their own living, is a matter ef national obligation, and not only of public charity. No one wishes to shirk this responsibility or to throw it upon the hospitals or other institutions, and it is to be hoped that we are not to have a repetition of the sad stories with which we have been familiar for years, with regard to old Crimean heroes, and others from India, who have been left he their own hard tate. The Medical Press seems to be el opinion that a course of Mafekine diet would be rather beneficial than otherwise. Those people in search of a hygieniceseastros nomy might try it, but it must be confessed that the experiences of the garrison are hardly likely to make horseflesh more popular as an article of diet. Of course what is meant is, that a period of semi-starvation is in many cases,a enol thing, and thaugh it was bad for the sick and wounded, the remarkable fit condition of the Mafeking garrison in the last days of the seige, when it. soundly beat the Boerferather tends to confirm this view Many people says the "Hospital," habitually consume not only more food that they require, but more than is good for them. Tbe truth of this is becoming more and more recognised, and even in the houses of the wealthy, what the doctors call" plain food" is gradually t king the place of the more elaborate cuisine. The London season is bow in full swing, and by no means the failure predicted some time since. Balls so far, have been few and far between and entertainments generally far from plentiftfl, but what with charity bazaars, charity concerts, and fashionable restaurant dinners, at which everybody who is anybody congre- gates, and talks" war news" the season is proving a very enjoyable if compaeatively, quiet one. The •' rest " cure is now extensively patronised by Society women, who in addition to the customary Saturday to Monday jaunt to some quiet country retreat make a point of spending at least ore day out of every fourteen, during their town season, in bed. Many are adding to the" rest " the " herb cure "the result being such that remarkably few cases of " make up " are es evidence. Among the now popular herb teas, or " simples" as country folks term them, a decoction manufactured from nettles, and another from eye-bright are perhaps in greatest favour. Herb gardens and still rooms are quite a feature of country houses just now, and the demand for old time recipe books, far exceeds the supply. Althcugh the cycle is no longer patronised in town by the fashionable woman, in the country it remains her favourite means of locomotion. In this particular she but follows the example of ruany of our Princesses, who have by no means abandoned the cycle for country I use. The Princess of Wales and her three daughters, are all enthusiastic cyclists still, as are also the young Prin- cesses of Connaught, Princess Victoria of Schleswig Holstein, and Princess Ea of Bettenberg. Undoubtedly cycling, fencing, rowing, golf, tennis, etc., have had the effect of increasing the SiZ3 of our hands and feet. A five and three-quarter, or eix glove is a comparative rarity nowadays, the maj ,rity of us baying to acknowledge a six and a quhrfer, half, or three-quarter glove, and a fcur or perchance five shoe. as being necessary to our requirements. But better far a larger hand and foot, with improved health and com- plexion, than the old time order of things, when robust health, and an excellent appetite were deemed vulgar indeed. Smart society has discovered a new diversion which is nothing less than to exhibit itself on the staeo. Several women of fashion have in times past gone on the stage, whilst others have left the stage for the higher circle,,' but now it seems ladies of wealth and fashion are to appear in the new ballet at the Empire Theatre of Varieties, as an addition to the alterations of that popu- lar Hall in London. The applicants for the dczeu or more places in the ballet which will be entitled "Ou the Beach " include several peeresses, and society biauties, 'and they are of course to" walk on" in the latest Con- fections, and the smartest of summ,r frocks. They are to be engaged for a fixed period at tkle usual professional salaries, and will afford a first class opportunity of studying the latest costume! for the forthcoming pier and promenade season at the seosid?. The gown that boasts no bolero is almost a curiosity and exclusive modistes are turning their attention to fresh fields and pastures new, as regards the cot of this Iparticular addition to our teilette. The latest is Cut SO I short in front as to be nothing more than a yolk sloping under the arms towards the back, win re it finishes in long coat tails. A few have appeared lately at garden iparties, and bazaars' over muslin waisrceets and skirts of the same billowy fabric, but the fact remains that although this form of bolero is a very novel one,the old familiar style is much more becoming to the majerity. While some women are much be-rufilsd—almost beyond recognition--others are dispinsing with neck furniture altogether. A tiny frill finishes tbe top of the bodice or blouse, a single raw of pearls taking the plac of the collar band. On a warm summer's day tee idea undoubtedly makes for comfort, and is pictureN3e too. provided, of course, the nrck be white and well shaped, and the face above prstty and young. Women less favoured should restrict themselves to semi-transparent ryokes and &slier bands, while others not favoured at all should indulge in flesh or other coloured lininge, which impart, at least, a cool appearance to a Wong". Someone made the funeral of Sir George Grove, the occasion for what Johnson described es helping forward the general disgrace of humanity. The Prince and Prin. cal Of Wales sent a wreath with a card beering the words "As a token of respect and regard." Soon after, when the mourners had left the cemetery, it was die- covered that the card had been remevei That is, it had been stolen,lri all probability by some scciety tuft hunter, who would not scruple at any crime or meanness in order to gain sech a prize. Gooseberry Charlotte.—Butter a pie dicta, c ,ver the bottom and sides of it with thin slices of buttered bread, place some stewed gooseberries sweetened, then bread and butter again, and Proceed with tbe.e layers till the dish is full. Bake in a quick oven for 20 minutes, turn lon to a dish, sift sugar over, and serve. "BUDGE."

div.head: WARRINGTON WORKMAN'S
div.p: A WARRINGTON WORKMAN'S
COMPENSATION,
Application for a Review.

Before U Elonour Judge wynne James at the War- rington County Court last Thursday,the case of Messrs. Joseph Crosfieid and Sons, United v. Patrick 'Fenian was again brought forward. In August of last year Tanian was awarded compensation amounting to 123 6d a week for the loss of an eve whilst working in the caustic department at Messrs. Crosfield's works. The award was based on the statement that the workman was receiving 303 a week at the time of the accident; but it was now urged that his wages only averaged 193 mv per week and an application was made for the order to be reviewed.—Mr. Langdon, barrister, Mancheeter, aepeared on behalf Of the applicants and Mr. Forshaw represented the workman.—Mr. Langdon in making his application admitted that the cate was really being fought by the Insurance Company and that it was practically a test case. His Honour in giving judgment reviewed the facts of, the case. He said it was an applicatien under rub o 12 Shedule I,Uf the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1597, to vary an award made by his predecessor. Mr. Langdon admitted that the position of the workman was precis- by the same as it was at the time his predecessor made the award and that in no respect had the circumstances and facts altered since the time the award was given. He was asked to open the award by going into the evidence as regarded what the weekly earnings of the man were at the time of his accident. It was suggested that the particulars put in by the applicant (the workman) at the time of the award were incorrect ; that be was not earning the sum he there stated but a lesser amount. Mr. Langdon asked rermission to tender that evidence in Court to day. He admitted however, that that evid- ence he was prepared to give and would have given it at the time of the arbitration had his answer been filed in time or permission given to file it. He (his Honour) was of opinion that that evidence was not admissible on the following grounde. —Rule 12 of schedule one was placed in the Act for the purpose of enabling an arbitrator to alter an award where tbe circumstances had altered since the time ot the award. They might have altered in respect of the workman improving in health and being able to earn his full wagrs and therefore enabling the Court to lessen the amount of the weekly payment which had been awarded or put it away entirelv. On the other hand circum- stances might have altered by the workman becoming more seriously ill and being totally incapacitated. lu those circumstances it would be opsn for the County Gaud Judge not to diminish out to increase the amount the workman ought to receive. He admitted that the terms of rule 12 were extremely general, - but he was of opinion that at all events the main purpose for which that rule was passed was the one he had mentioned, and therefore the applicants were precluded from giving evidence at the present time. If his decision would be otherwise, there was nothing to prevent an employer not putting in any answer to the application for arbitration, and even not attending court if he thought fit although ho bad evidence ready, and apply at the very next Court to call evidence to show that the award should be reviewed, although he might with due dili;.ence have given it at the time. He could not think that this was the intention of the legislature. He bad admitted Mr. Langdon'a evidence under protest because if the case should go to a court of appeal it might not be necessary to hold a second in- quiry in Warrington. If that evidence were admissible he was not satisfied that the award of the County Court Judge was a wrong one. It was admitted that previous to the award the respondent wes receiving 12i 61 a week. That at all events was some evidence, it not strong evidence, that it was 50 per cent. of his wages. He should regair3 much stronger evidence to pet aside or vary the award. Coats would be allowed on B scale.

div.head: MR SPEIGHT LIGHTS HIS PIPE.
div.p: MR SPEIGHT LIGHTS HIS PIPE.
Thera lay Mr. Robert Speight's pipe on the shelf, black and cold as an ancient Aztc altar. He had not taken a pull on it for days; he said he didn% enjoy it any m ore.
Now a Nun may have a row with a friend, and the two meet without speaking f•Jr six months, ye: no harm done.

To throw off one's smoke, however, is a different thing ;it is a bad sign. Oar friend oad not repudiated tobacco on what is called " principle ;" he had not joined any of these societies you know—the sort that enjoy themselves by making ottE,rs mi,er able—and then give out that the Millen- ium is close ab rard. Not a bit of that. Ile loved his fragrant old brierwood with undiminished devotion, but—well, takd the tale right from his own mouth—it will hit a lot of us on the side of the head where W 2 most need a little sense knocked in.

"The whole mattvr," says Mr. Speight, in a letter dated December 12;.h, 1899, " tots up at this. I had been a chronic: dyspeptic for five years. My life was dismal as a rainstorm that never lets up. I had such awful headaches I could hardly attend to business. I had wretched nights, and days off the same piece. My tongue wa3 coated deep wail fur ; and the taste in the month, especially in the morning, was at to sicken a Greenlander.

" Most of the time tiv,ro was a dull, heavy pain in the left side. and a feeling ot tightness across the chest, as though an iron band were screwed around me. I was afraid to eat anything a olid tecause it gave me the sense of chairing ; and whenever I did eat pastry, cr roast or fried meat, I couldn't stand the feeling it gay() me. I was obliged to make myself sick with salt and water and get relief that way. For months together I lived on slops. "Thinking it might do the good I went with some friends to the Isle of Man for 'a hi 'ay, but was glad to get back. Dsctors attended 111:3, tnu . their mediernes all missed the mark. I could no lonier enjoy my pipe, and this lefc me lonely as a wrecked sailor; all smokers Viill nderstand tha I.

"When I had made up my mind I was booked to suffer to the end of my dye, I firr read abmt the cures done by Miter Seigel's Syrup. Ttefirt bottle gave me grea t relief, and two more made a pr- fectly well man of me. It is a pleasure now for me to work, and my old pipe is once more in constant service. My opinion ef M Ater Seigel's Syrup may be inferred from whit I have aid. Nowadays I eat and digest pastry and evcret hing else that comes my way."—Robcrt .SPeigni, Draper, 2, Rlchardshaw-Line, Pudsey, Yorke.

div.p: A LOCAL DOCTOR AND HIS DUTIES. Claim for Negligence against Dr. Parker.

An interesting case was beard at the Warrington County Court last Thurseay, before His Honour Judge Gwynne James, in which De J. T. Paiker, of Stockton Heath, claimed the sum of £4 lOs 6d frem John Pembe-s ton, builder and brick manutacturer,for professional ser- vices. There was a counter claim for £5 damages. Caused by the negligence of the plaint if in not attending defendant when he had promised to oo so.—Mr. Bro ne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Langdon barrister (instructed by Mr. Forsha w) represented the defendant. Dr. Parker was called, and stated that he was a duly qualified medical practitiener at Stockton Heath. The nefendant owed him £4 10i 6J balance for professional services. Cross-examined by Mr. Langdon : Mr Pemberton lived near to witness, and had known bim for some Years. He had been his medical attendant. On the 10th Of April at 7 Cclock in the morning, the defendant's sister came to him and asked him to attend to Mr. Pem- berton, as he had sustained an injury to his leg. Sue asked for a piaster. Did you ask her why she had come so early in the Morning P-1 asked why she had not sent for me the evening before. Did you tell her that you would call and see her brother a little later on —I cannot remember. What do you remember saying ?—I said to her " I did not send you a plaster because it would not be pro- Per treatment. "She said to me "Will you see him ?' Her manner was such that I said " Why didn't you send , for me yesterday evening," and ,o far as I remember I gave her no deckled answer as to whether I should see His Honour: D;d you not give a decided answer that 1c3,11 should see him.—l only treaded that I should not 11'145 him the plaster. e His Honour : Never mind that. Did you give a decided -41':Ivier that you should see him some time ?—Witness : „,I5 very possible that I did. eft With examined witness said that defendant's sister 'ea with that impression and he knew it. Mr. Langdon: Didn't she tell you that her brother had met with an accident last night and had had great pain all night bat he did not wish to disturb you in the night time.—She said that in answer to my inquiry. Didn't she come again about an hour .nd a half later and ask you why you did not come ?—No ; she did uot speak to me. Did the servant bring a message asking why you did not come? Yes. What did you say in reply? I made no answer. Do you mean to sa, that you gave no answer at all? sent her a b x of ointm,,nt. What did you say ? I said nothing. Did you tell the servant that you would come pre sently—No. Did you intend coming presently ?—}lo. Why riot? Because of toe manner in which she came to the door. She rang the bell in a very insulting Way. His Honour: Rang the bell in an insulting way. What do you meaa P—She rang it very loudly and spoke to the servant in an impudent manner. His Honour: I want to know why you did not go afterwards—When she came the second time she said to the servant, tell him that if it is to much trouble for bun to come I will very soon get eomeone that will. His Honour: Why did not you answer her. Didn't You think it was a very natural thing for her to say. You must be very touchy —Mr. Pemberton had been Sending for me for the last three years without paying the bill. Mr. Langdon : Atl2 30 did not the defendant's niece, Emily Atkin come P-1 do not know anything abut that When did you get to know that she had been P—ln the afternoon. I was interviewed on another occasion by his clerk. His Honour: Was the clerk impertinent P—No he Was not at all. What did you say to him ?—I said I should prefer Mr. Pemberton to confee his patronage on some otter doctor. He had employed me sufficiently long enough and he had better share his benefits valeta someone else. His Honour : Somewhat satirical. (Laug er.) Further examined witne-s admitted that he i d had a Contra account with Mr Pemberton for work dude. He sent his collector to Mr Pemberton for the account. The Only occasion on which he had sent the collector was after the trouble took place. You never asked for payment until after this event? --A doctor is not supeo,ed to do. His Honour : A decter is not supposed to ask for his be a P—Not personalty. He must be a very thin skinned doctor. Do you mean You have never asked for fees ? —No. It had better b known in Warrington. (Laughter.) Mr.Langdon: When your collector got home did not he bring yeu this message from Mr.Pemberton."Why has Dr. Parker sent you : I want to go and see him about hie not coming to see me before I pay his bill." At the time you sent your collector . was he not lying in bed Still sufferieg from his injuries ?—I did cot know that. Did yea r )w what was the matter with him P—l inferred what was the matter with him. The second time his sister ce MP I seet a bex of antiseptic ointment Which was per z,ct treaLment. His Honour asked why he did not tell defendant's sister that he was not coming. Witness: She was gme by the time I came downstairs. Further questioned he said he should have seen Mr. Pemberton during She morning if his sister had not behaved in that manner the second time. Florence Pemberton said that she went to see Dr. Parker at seven o'clock. He said he could not give her anything until be had seen her brother and he would Come later on. She called again about an: hour and a half later and saw the servant and asked her if she would ask the (leder when Le was coming. The servant brought her a box of ointment but did not say anything. By Mr. Browne : She old not tell the servant that if Dr. Parker did not coaie she would get, some no Ise, bot did she speak in a very head tone. The bell was an electric bell, aud they bed to rill it loudly. Dr. Braid. %rem called be Mr Browne, and said that he ;tag calleci in to see Mr. Pemberton between three and our o'clock.fle found him to be suffering from abrasions 9f the skin caused by ~roshing. It was not a serious leajurY. He attended him for ten diva, and ordered him lotion to ease the pair. He could not say that Mr. retnberton would have been able to go out earlier if Dr

Pa-ker had attended him in the morning. Mr. Browne contended that a doctor was not bound to attend a patient as a necessity. He sub -nit•ed ha, if a man came to him and said be wantel to be attended to and gave him a guinea for doing 50 that was a oontract that wsaild be compulsorily carried out. If he came to the doctor a'nf said he wanted him to attend to tomeone, if the doctor said he would come he was not bound to do eo, as there was no contract. Not one doctor in the town would attead unless he pleased, unless there was a contract between them. His Honour : I el:lite agree that a doctor is entitled to sap "Under the circumstances I will not attend" bu it is nnt right to say "I will attend" and not come. Th law of England is not different to the law of Warrington There are a number of cases where doctors have b-en held liable. Mr. Browne said that if he had cornmencel to attend he admitted that was so. He had not, however, com- menced and the messenger being impudent he refuted to go. Hi, Honour asked why the doctor did not say he would Lot attend Mr. Browne said the woman had gone before he cmAl get downstairs. Mr. Pemberton could not prove any damage. He dare not call Dr. Braide to prove that he had sustained any damage from Dr. Parker not attending. It would be a most serious thing for doctors ia the town if hi.; Honour held that he was liable to damages br—ause he did not attend. The damage was very small ana very remote.

He Honour summed up at considerable length. I He quite agreed that a doctor under oruinary circumstances need not attend any par, icular individual if he refused to do so. That WAI a general proposition but there were exceptions even te that rule which it was unnecessary for him to go into. He found in the present case the following facts proved before him Mr. Pemberton had received cer- tainly serious injury by having his leg celestial on the evening of the 9:h April. He did not at the time think it was very serious, but as the pain incre-eed during the night so that he could not Bleep he realiz,d in the morning that his position was a serious one. He sent his sieter to Dr. Parker. The poeition of Dr. Parker and Mr. Pemberton had been a most friendly one. He had been the family doctor for some years, and not only that but they had been mutual friends. Under the circumstances there was not a more proper person to go to for assistanc3 than the family doctor who had also been & friend of Mr. Pemberton. The yeung lady arrived at 7 o'clock in the morn- ing. The first thing the doctor said was, "You should have sent for me earlier than this ; you ought to have sent for me the night before." She replied that they did not wish to trouble him earlier. Realizing the importance of an early visit he intimated to the young lady that he was coming round to see her brother. For some reason or other he did not go. Mr. Pemberton of course relied upon his doctor carrying out the intimation to his sister. Tne sister was sent again an hour afterwards. She rang the bell and asked for the doctor to come. The doctor heard or he was Sold that there was a disturbance in the hall aad lost his temper. It appeared as if the lady acted as the pro- verbial red flag did to the bull. The reason the doctor gave was that she rang the bell in an insulting way and in a loud voice told him that if he could not come she would get same one else. He, however, did not intimate that he would not attend the man. A message was sent later on by some other relative and a fourth message was sent by the clerk. Dr Parker then for the first time considered it consistent with his position to say be would not attend simply because he had lost his temper with the young lady who rang the bell violently. Under Those circum- stances Mr Pembertoa asked for damages. It was sug- gested that there was no contract, but he (his flow or) thought there was a contract to begin with. Mr Pemberron relied upon Dr Parker coming and did not call in another doctor and Dr Parker would expect to be paid if he went there. Even if there wasnot a contract it was his bounden duty, moral and legal, to have kept his word and to have attended his old friend as he ntimated to the sister that he would. Mr Browne said t would be a serious thing for the doctors in the town It would be a Serious thing for the inhabitants it I doctors could intimate that they would come and ;Wend them when they were seriously ill and did not do so. The only other point was as to whether Mr. Pemeerton had suffered any damage. Dr. Braide was called by Mr. Browne and he admitted that Mr. Pember- ton would have suffered less if the doctor had been sent for. That was the opinion of Dre Parker because he sug- gested that he should have been sent for the day before. Immediately on the lotion being administered the atient was relieved. He found on these facts that Mr. Pemberten had suffered pain which he would no, otherwise have suffered if he had been properly attended to be Dr. Parker in the :norning. He gave judgment for toe plaintiff on the cle and for the defendant on the counterclaim, costs to velem each. Counsel's fee was also Bowed. Mr. Browne asked for leave to appeal on the ground that there being no contract the doctor was not bound to attend. Hie Honour : I ruled against him because the doctor said he would attend. I most certainly ...deice ie Confirming, he considered there had been a contract, tee contract being that the defendant would not employ any • tee r doctor. It was his gat and moral duty, having Lir mised to attend, to do so.

BLOWING THE GAS OUT.—A Devon farmer iIaITIECI Robert Chaning, who lived near Tiverton, went to Bath for the waters. Next morning be was found nearly suffocated with gas, the burner in his bedroom being turned on. Be died on Tuesday. Elia relatives say that be was unaccustomed to gas, and there is every reason to suppose that he blew it out. At the inquest yesterday a verdict of death from gas poisneine was returned. THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JUNE 8,1900.
THE NEW WORKHOUSE INFIRMARY.
The Opening Ceremony

There was a representative gathering of ladies and gentlemen of the town and district at the opening proce idings. Sir J T Hibleert accompanied by Dr J M Ritodee (President of the Ai,secieti on of Poor Law Unions of England and Wales). Mr A J J >Bey, chairman of the Board of Guardians, together with the members and officials assembled at the front entrance of the Infirmary at 3 o'clock. Many well known public men connected with the Town Council and other local bodies also withessed the proceedings. Amongst them 'nay be named the member for the Borough, Mr R Pierpoint, M.P. Mr John White, J.P., Mr F Monks, J.P., Council- lor William Pierpoint, J.P., Revs E R Tarbuck, H V Pilot, Father Ryan, John Yonge, T Bishop, and J H Riddette. Toe CIIAIRMAN of the Board who was cordially received said it gave him vary great pleasure to see suca an assemblage representing the people of Warrington and the neiehbouring district to take part in the ceremony of opening that large and import ant building, the new Infirmary. On behalt of his colleagues on the Board of Guardians he cordially welcome I all who had honoured them with their presence. Especially did he thaele for their presence to-day Sir John Hibbert and Dr. Rhodes. The last named was the head of an important organiza- tion, the Association of Poor Law Uaions of England and Wales. But not otly as head of that did he welcome him, but because he had gained for himself not mere y a national, but a Euro- pean reputation as a Poor Law reformer. (Efsar, hear.) If it were possible even more warmly did he thank his old friend Sir John Hibbsrt. He was a veteran reformer who had won his reputation years ago by taking an active part in almost every form of social work. He had devoted himself to the comns in good dur- ing the long years of an honourable life and in almost every department of work from the B iard of Guardians up to the Treasury Bench he had dieeinguished himself. For a quarter of a ceetury there hid b ten in existence an organization in this part of the country called the North Western Peer Law Cenference of which he had ben President from the beginning. In that position he had not only striven to promote efficiency in Poor LAW Administration but to arouse public interest in an intelligent way in Poor Law matt Ts. I WAS greatly to be regretted that unfortunately there was not that intelligent intereet is Poor LAW adininieration which the importance of the eubject demanded. He did not say this because he was a Poor Law Guardian but because he felt that there was a grave danger that so impertarit a breech had not always received that recognition from the general body of the community which it ought to have had. There seemed to be an opinion that anyone was good enough for a Poor Law Guardian. (L aughter ) No Opinirt ciaulii be more dangerous and disastrous than that. (Elear, hear.) Tee work was of great aocial im- portance in many ways and if they got gentlemen or ladies—for they had lady guardians now he WAS glad to say—who undertook this work without having counted the cost at the outset they were too often disheartenei. The amount of detail work which Boards of Guardians had to perform was very great indeed and *as very often diseouraging to those who entered upon the work in a somewhat enthusiastic spirit. The ideal Guardian should have a warm heart and a cool head as well. (Hear, hear). Procesding to refer to the new infirmary be said it was not for him to select any individual Guardian for special praise, a number of them having shared the burden, but he thought he should be lacking in his duty to his colleagues were he not to bear testimony to the worm of the chairman of the Infirmary and Buildings Committee, Mr William Houghten, who had given freely of his time and energy to the work. (Applause). }Mere proceeding to the other portion of the cere- mnny. he would aek the Chaplain oa the Workhouse,the Rey. E R Tarbuck, to invoke a divine blessing on the work. Tue Rev. E. R. TARSUCK then offered prayer. Mr. WILLIAM EIOUGATON, as Chairman of the In- firmary Coniitattee afterwards handed to Sir J. T. Hi bbort a gold key with which to open the entrance doer. In doing so be said that the Infirmary had been provided to give better accommodation and greater comfort for those who had to seek its shelter. As Sir John knew. they had a continual influx of sink and infirm people. They also got a number of temporary eases which came here as the result of accident or sickness. Continuing, he said that the Guardians hoped that by the means afforded by the new Infirmary they would be able to tiring tneir patients inure quickly to convalescence and be able to restere them more rapidly to their families and friends. They had also a great number who came there never to see the outside again. They were enabled by the improved cenditioes which weuldexist at the Infirmary to mitigate their sufferings. The subject of building the new infirmary, had been under the consideration of the Board of Guardians for a long time, and new th: t it was finished helenped it would fulfil all that was intended. He might also allude to the fact that the Board of Guardians had from their ex• teerience in past years, thought it well to provide for a eupply of nurses. They were providing there for a number of probationers and he thought ie was a move- ment in the right direction. On behalf of the Board of Guardians of the Union he bad the honour to ask Sir John's acceptance of the key. (Applaut,e.)

Sir J. T. HIBBERT then opened the entrance door with the above magnificent 18-carat gold key which is of most artistic design, the stein being quite plain .whilst the handle is round and elegantly mounted with massive scrolls. In the centre is an enamelled shield bearing the borough arms, surrounded by a wreath. The outer circle is of pale blue enamel and gold relief, with the following words thereon :—" Warrington Union New lofirmary." On the reverse side is the monogram c f the recipient in gold, and engraved on the b irder en- circling this is the inscription—" Preset tfd to Sir J. T. Hibbert, K.C.B ehairman of the Lancashire County Council, May, 1900." The work of designing and manufacture was en- trusted to R. C. Oldheld, the renowned jeweller and sileersmith, of Liverpool. L Sir JOHN HIBBERT then addressed the gathering. He said he hoped he had performed the duty which led been placed upon him in a satisfactgry and workman like manner. It showed that the Guardians of the Warrington Union were so thorough that even the gold key which they bad placed in his hands wss able to open the door for future usefulness. (Appiause). He could only express the hope that all woo might come within the walls of that institution might be relieved, and that though the' might not, be restored to entire health, they might be enabled to be saved from some of eam, eufferings which they might have otherwise under- one had they not come within those walls and in some cases permitted to rejoin their families. He loeked upon that institution as a great credit to the Guardians of the Warrington Union. There were only a very few of the Unions of this country who had established institutions like that apart from their workhouses. Though it would cost the ra'opayers something like £35,000 he could assure them that they bad never made a better invest nent. He believed that there was no surer way of reducing pauperism than by having institutions cf this character. The infirmary would be used by poor pe3ple who were broken down in health either through accident or other causes, and the sooner they enabled a wet king man or working woman to return to employment the more surely they were laying the foundation of restoOog them to independence. ' Beer 'mar.) He was afraid quit in these prosperous times the people who were t.ecitiving largo wages were not saying be what they oegbt to do for a rainy day. It was unfnrtunate tor them in that respect. As an old Guardian he could not eeeoid referring the ,ut!eat. He trust( d that LI future years the spirit of thrift would more and more engraved upon the hearts ot neople. (Applause.) Be did not suppose ther as a harder working people in the world than the p pie of England, and if the people of England were hero working there was not a mere hard working people than the people of Lancashire (Hear. hear.) He did not wish to deny the people of Lencashire their pleasures, sports, and amusements,but he hoped they would remember that they bad a responsi- bility cast upon them which was even greater than that of amusement and that of their own pleasure, and that was providing for the future for the memlers of the families they bring up. Be was glad to think that there Was a much greater spirit of thrift amongst thew than there was in times past. U they went back to 1834,

when the Act was passed for the reform of the poor , laws, there was scarcely an able bodied man in the country who was not receiving re'ief in some form or other, either in aid of his wigs or the rent of his cottage, and had those times gone on the landowners and property owners would have been eaten up and the recipients themselves would have suffered with it. Since 1834 they had had a m ore humane system in the administration of the poor laws, and those engaged in that administration were to be thanked for their lab iurs . (Bear, hear). As the Chairman had said, the duties of a Poor Law Guticlian were not pleasant. They were very disagreeable at times and therefore it was a credit to our country that there were so many gentlemen Who cetne forward day by day, week by wetk and month by month and carried out this work which had been entailed upen them by the Parliament of the country. He would say all honour to them for what they had done. (Hear. hear.) He had been a Poor Law Guardian for 25 years and he believed that the training he got in the Board of Guardians enabled him to do better work in the greater Board of Guardians sitting in Parliament than ,he should have been able to do had he not received that previous train- ing. (Hear, hear.) He merely mentioned that ti !show tnat he still viewed matters as a Guardian and as long as he had health and strength he hoped he might be able to devote hi:nself to matters of importance in the administration of the Poor laws in this country. Pro- ceeding to refer to the erection of infirmaries in connec- tion with workhouses, Sir John Hibbert said he believed Liverpool had the credit of being the pioneer in the erection of infirmaries with properly trained nurses. He could not mention Liverpool without introducing the name of Mr. William Rathbone—(applause.)—who for several years gave two or three thousands pounds per year towards the training of nurses. • He was glad t S think that they were getting rid of the Sarah Gimp class of nurse in their workhouse infirmaries, and that the time was not far distant when they would be with out pauper nurses. It wa a only 25 years ago that the sick in workhouses were attended to by the piaupera themselves, but they were now being rapidly superceded by the trained nurses, some of whom he was pleased to see present. (Applause.) He found in the last return of the Local Government Board that 38 proposals were made during the year for the enlargement or erection of infirmaries, all at con- siderable cost. He netieed that one hospital in London was estimated to cost £204,000. He was glad to find ia the list that there were six or seven proposals for in- firrnaries in Lancashire. In connection with that matter let him call their attention to the cost of admioisterirr, the Poor Law* Forty years ago we spent on the poor of this clunl•ry £5,80 0,000, but it had now increased to £10,800,000. Much of the increased cost was due to the c ei- ef lunatics. In 18e8 while lunatics only cost £377,000 in 1898 they cost £1,700,000. Great 89 was the incfease in the cost of administering the poor laws the money was not wasted in giving out-relief bat in the provision of more comfortable workhouses, the pro- vision of workho use hospitals, and even where there ' were no Infit melees, in making better provision for the sick. If they rememo red for one moment what the drink bill of this country was they -woal I see that the cost of the relief of the poor was a rners flea-bite to it. I'm drink biil amounted to over £130,000,000, whereas. the Coit of relieving the poor wes oely £10,800.03J They need not be afraid of putting their hands in their pockets for an erection of this kind. (Hear, hear). Perhaps at some future time the Guirdans would enter- tain the sugeestion of having a resident medical officer on the premises With the help of trained nurses he was certain that alleviation of suffering w mld be given to the unfortunat persons who came within those walls. (Hear, hear.) While talking with respect to the sick let him say one word on the education of the young. If there were two things the Guardians ought to have credit for it wag thet they not only tended the sick but also the education of the young He believed that by means of good education they would permanently reduce the ranks rot pauperism. (Applause.) He had been up to Padget° Schools during the day and he did not know that he had ever seen a more agreeable, pleasing and happy sight than the children in that institution. He had the privilege of sesiag the boys and , girls at dinnereand from all he saw in the Institution he should say that they would become good members of society. (Hear, fe-ate) He mentioned this to show that the Guardians were doing their duty and thil nublic were indebted to them for tho work they did. 11-.! had great pleasure in b.mili,,, there that day to help in the opening of that Institution. fl felt it to be an honour and hoped this town and all witnin it would long continue to pro per in future years as they had done in the past. (Applause. Mr. GEORGE PILLING proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Sir -John Ilitobeec ;or his presence and said they were under an obligation to him for making the journey. Mr. Josane BALL seconded the proposition which was heartily carried. ..

Sir JOHN HIBBERT in acknowledging the compli- ment, said he forgot to express his gn it satisfction that they had in the Warrington Unlon two lady Guardians who were present that day. About twenty-five years ago there was only one lady Guardian in ttie country, and she was elected in connection with a London Union. Now there were 800 lady Guardians all over the country, and they were doing the work much better tan the men c)uld do it. (Laughter and applause). The opening proceedings then terminated.

div.head: WARRINGTON ENGINEDRIVER AND HIS WORRIES
div.p: A WARRINGTON ENGINE- DRIVER AND HIS WORRIES

It is not everybody who would like to be the driver of a locomotive, and furthermore ic is not everybody who possesses the capability for the post even if he had the inclination. No ! there is generally something excep- tional about the man who is put in charge of a railway engine. Wa have good reason to respect engine drivers. Firtt and foremost tnev have charge of our own precious lives, and in addition we know they are men of honesty, coutage. and sobriety—qualities which are still rare enough to be admired. There are plenty of engine drivers in Warrinetnn, men who have won their onerous positions by persever- ance and hard work. Some of them go out daily on the huge railroads which intersect the town, and others are employed in the harassing task of shunting in the yards of the big manufactories It was with one of the engine-drivers of this class that a reporter of the" Warrington Esaminer," recently bad a conversation.
MR. JAMES EVANS. Front a Photograph by Parkinson, Warrington. _

Mr. James Evans, 9, WeHold-street. Warrington, is an engine-driver-in the employ of Mesers. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, one of the largest enan.making firms in th, world, and heis a man who takes an interest in his w,) t. As he is 49 years of age he has had eome experience and knows that the best of health is neessary for him ogo through his day's work But the Lest of heslt is not easily procurable and is onlv possessed by the favoured few. Mr. Evans has not been one of the fay.eured few during the six or seven years he had ,been working at Warrington. He was troubed very much by in- digestion, and pains in the side, for which he took much medical advice and a large quantity of so-called curatives without deriving much benefit Then, about four months ago the influenza fiend claimed him as a victim and brought him down to such a low state that he was three weeks absent from work. His previous complaint remained,of course. In his own words, "I got terribly low, and always felt more tired when I had done nothing. than I shoeie have done if I had done a laboririue day's work The pain in my side was there ten. While i we in this state a pamphlet entitled" The Way to Be Well" was pushed under my door, and that gave me an idea. I would try Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people, and I wrote to the firm straight away and got a box. From the first 1 had faith in the eills, and by the time I had finished two or three box. a i felt much better and stronger. Before, I had not been able to keep warm, but now I got warmer and gained strength rapidly. The pain in my side wont away altogether, and I gained Wes. weight in six weeks. I have been better in health since then than I have been all the six years I have lived iu Warrington." Questioned more particularly about cit indigestion trouble, Mr. Evans said he had not felt it since he took the pills, and " I can eat anythine now Thank God! and Fleep well too." In conclusion, he added with a smile of content" I can go through a day's work with pleasure now." Before leaving, the reporter learnt from the com- municative engine-driver that he had recommended Dr. Williams' pink pills to several friends of his, and had even gone so far as to buy them a box or two himself. His wife, he said, had been a great sufferer from sick headaches for many years and he had persuaded her to try the pills. Though she had only been taking them a short time she was already feeling considerable benefit, and he hoped she would be cared altogether. Oefore the reporter left, Mr. Evans gave him permission to publish these facts, for, said he, os I _should like people to benefit if they can only be told.'

div.head: WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB.
Annual Amateur Athletic Sports.

was perhaps impossible for the first annual Amateur Athletic Sports in connction with the Warrington Cricket Club,held on th Arpley Cricket Ground on Saturday, to have taken place under more favourable auspices. The weather was gloriously flue, the track was in capital condition and there was a most encouraging att,endance of the public. Admirable arrangements had been made by the officials for the revival of this one-time annual festival and an attractive program ne was the out- come of their labours. It was generally azread by the spectators that the cricket ground was splendidly adapted for the put pose and the proceedings pissed off with such gratifying success that the sports will no doubt become an annual function. It is somewhat unfortunate that on this occasion not a single prize was won by a Warring competitor, but we must hope for better luck next time. The entlies numbered 370, the competitors including a number of "crack' athletics. Wads.ey,o7 Loadon.the 100 and 440 yards Eagiish chanapile was accorded a hearty reception. He entered the 100 yards and 220 yards flat races and was scratch man in each event. In the 100 yards he was beat.m by J. A. Cadman of Ard wick who had a start of 7i yards. Children's Treat at Houghton. On Monday afternoon, Mrs. Geo:go Mather, of Cinnamon Farm, Fearnhead, gave her annual treat to the children residing in the townsAps of Houghton, Middleton and Arbury. The children arrived at the farm shortly after two o'clock, and sat down to a good tea, their wanzs being amply supplied by Mr. and Mrs. Mather and a few friends. Afterwards several games and sports. took place in the farm yard and in a field, and nuts and sweets were distributed, and a very enj iyable afternoon and evening were spent. Whit-Monday at Warrington. Ideal weather prevailed on Whit Monday. The morning opened bright and fine, and the sun shone out brilliantly. The buyinees premies and works being closed, the people took the opportunity of visiting the seaside and other places. From an early hour the Cheshire Lines Railway were busy, the outgoing trains for Liverpool, Hauhester, New Brighton and Southport,and other places being well filled. The London and North-Western Railway at Bank Quay were just as busy, people travelling to all parts of Wales, Blackpool, and the north of England. Those who remained in town were catered for at the theatres and circus, where attrac- tive programmes were submitted. LA.THST DE3IGICS and colourings in Prints. At two o'clock a procession of children was formed at the Risley Presbyterian S3IIOOI, and, headed by the Warrington affougn Band, paraded the village and afterwards went to the farm. At four o'clock a good tea was provided. A mile bicycle race took place at three o'clock, for wnich there were six entries the winner being Mr It.)wlands. of Leigh. Griffon. the band- master, after which all the childr,n returi4ed to the school for the dancing, Mr. James lienshaw supplying the music.
Warrington Man Drowned in the Ship Canal.

Mr. E, A. Wilite, deputy conner, conducted an inquiry at the Red Lion Inn on Monday afternoon, into toe circumgtances attending the death of William Monks (29), wr'r livt mon his married sister in Winwick-coad and whose body was found in the Ship Canal at Keck wick on Sunday morning. —The evidence was to the effict tut', the deceased, who was employed at Messrs. Fletcher, Russell,and Company's works, as a gas stove tester, was last seen alive on the night of the 25th May. He and a companion had been in a pub- lic-house for a couple of nours. Deceased had had three or four glas+es of beer but he was sober. He refused, however, to go home, and when pressed lay down in the road, where his companion left him. He regardsd the fact of his lying in the road not as evidence of his incapability to go nome, but of his determination not to go home. A relative stated that deeeased had a short time previously been ill wirh iofluenza. When de- ceased did not return to his sister's nouse, informa- tion was given to the Warrington police but nothing was heard until Sunday,when a man named Wilkin- son saw a body floating in the Ship Canal at Keck.- wick, and, recovering it with the a,sistance of P.C. Ellis, conveyed it to the Red 'ion Inn, where it was identified as that of dec-ased. The police found on the body 103 10d in cash; a silver keyless watch, and a silver chain, a pocket book and the rules .of a sick club.—A verdict of -7`, Found drowned," was retlirn-d.

The start, however, was by no means encouraging, Kershaw and Bro.vn being disposed of with only 27 on the board. A Tinsley and Wilmot, however, put a ,iifferant complexion on the game, taking the score to 91, wh,,ri the former was splendidly caught by Halnpaoa.
Witn 212 for eight 'wickets, the home team captain dosed the innings (this being the fourth time in snoceß- sive matches), Bert Sharp (56 not out) and Wilmot (46) being the cnief contributors.

Warrington 2nd and B4ughton Hall Ist engaged on the ground of the latter. The game resulted in a victory for Boughton by a majority of 70 runs, Hughes being instrumental in scoring 57 for the winners. Silcock contributed 66 to the Warrington total.
