div.head: FATALITY AT OLD QUAY
div.p: FATALITY AT OLD QUAY
RUNCORN.
The Inquest.

Shortly after ten o'clock on Friday night last a shocking fatality occurred in the Ship Canal at Old Quay Wharf, Runcorn. Tao barge Merlin was be- in4 discharged of a cargo of rock salt, and Thomas Brown, married man. Pool-lane, and Richard Sal- keld, Norfolk-street, were in the hold of the craft filling the" tubs." A tub weighing with the con- tents about 223wts. was being drawn up, when the bolt securing the chain to the cxane broke, aud the tub fell upon Browa who was in a stooping condition. die body was frightfully crushed, and death must nave been instantaneous. His remains were removed home on the police ambulance. On Saturday after- noon Mr E A Wnite, the deputy coroner, held an ha- -1 qaest at the police station. Mr Charles Dutton was foreman of the jury. There were present—Mr E R Graves, inspector of factories, Mr F J Norman. manager of the ViTiggs' Works, representing the United Alkali Company, and Mr F A Lake, repre- senting deceased's widow. Eden Brown, stated that she lived at 16, Pool-lane. Runcorn. and deceased was her husband. He was 53 years of age. She last saw him alive at 5.30 on Friday night. Ha was then going to his work. He was in good he tlth. Ile was brought home dead just before eleven o'clock the same night. William Brown stated that he was a crane driver at Wiggs' Works and lived in Canal-street, Runcorn. On Friday night, abaut twenty minutes to ten, witnees was driving the crane, which as emptying a cargo of rock salt from a barge. They were lifting it out of the hold by means of iron tubs. D ceased was in the hold filling the tubs. Witness was hoisting a tub up, and the bolt fastening the chain to the drum on the winch suddenly snapped, and the tut, chain and hook all fell into the hold. Whea he saw it falling he called out a warning. The tub would be about 21ft. high from the bottoen of the hold whoa the accident occurred. There were four men in the hold. Witness first of all went to the boat and finding a man was under the tub he ran to the works entrance for help. They lowered a rope with a hook on it, someone fastened it to the tub, and then they hoisted it up. The men went into the hold to try to get deceased out. Witness saw him brought out, and he was then dead. It was Woe crane man's duty to examine the chain, and this particular chain was exam- ined last Sunday by William Brown, Haniford Leach, and Thomas Moores. Mr. Turnbull, engineer also ex- . &mined tbe chain. It was all right so far as witness could see. He examined this particular bolt, and it appeared to be all right.—Tho Inspector :—What was the diameter of the drum ? Witness: About twelve inches.—What is the total length rot the chain ? About eight feet —How far from the bottom of the ship would you have to drag the tub before it lifted ? About eight feet. The tub was next the wall.—Did it strike anything when it lifted ? No Sir.—What is the weight of the tub? About 21 cwte.—By Mr. Norman: Tao tub was never 7, taken off the chain. After being hoisted it was tipped over and emptied. It was witness's duty to examine this chain. The chain was nearly half wound up when the bolt broke.

Richard Saikeld. labourer, employed at Wiggs' Works, and residing at 29, Norfolk-street, Runcorn, stated that en Friday night he was assisting to unload the barge Merlin, which had a cargo of rock s.lt. The other men with-him were lifted MaFsey, John Salkeld, and the deceased. They were all engxged filing tubs. Two were filling one tub, and two another. Each man took his turn at unhooking :the tubs. The deceased filled a tub about a quarter to ten, and it was hooked on, and witness gave tno signal for it to be hoisted. He was about six feet from the tub at the time. The rock salt was tipped it 4 loose, like small coal. While they were filling another tub the one which had been hoisted came dowiz upon the empty tub. It fell upon the deceased and killed him instantly. The tub also caught witness on the hands, and he was inscaaiNe for a few moments. When witness came round hi c.w the men trying to get at the deceased.

Alfred Massey, 6, Norfolk-street,gave similar evidence. The first thing witness heard was Richard Saikeld call out" Oh dear, oh dear." He looked round and saw one tub on top of the other. Witness said "Where's Brown?" and as Salkeld did not reply he went and .00ked and found deceased had been caught between tii 3 two tubs. Witness called out for assistancs. It would :aka six or eight men to lift a tub. The rope was li:wered, and the tub raised. Brown was then dead. Thomas Turnbull, engineer at Wiggs' Works, stated C•at he lived at Brindley Cottage. Irwell-lane. It was his duty to look after all the machinery right through the works. He examined the steam cranes every week thoroughly. He examined thio. particular crane about 11 o'clock on Friday wroing. The crane was then working. He examined it the previois Suniay morn- in about /0 o'clock. It was then stopped. He exam- ined all the parts ard found them all in order. There vra, b, flaw at the point where the bolt broke.—By the in.p•etor : Witrtss, when examining the crane, had lse bolt taken out and put on again. The drum was 11 inch thick. The bolt would go 1, bout a quarter of an inch through the drum. The breaking strain of the bolt would he from six to eight tons.—The In.nector: How I cluch oh ain wauld remain on the barrel after it had got to the bottom of the hoid.—Witnese : I should think about a turn and a half -[he chain had run out to its lull length many a time. How long had the chain been in use ?—I should think a bout six months. The hook and bolt had been in use 12 or 14- months.—By Mr. Norman : Every attention was paid, to the safety of the men, and Low Moor (the best) iron only was used for these things. It was tested before being used. Dr. McDougall said lie was called to see the deceased a., the ambulance room at the works shortly after ten o'clock. Ho was quite dead. He had since examined the body, and found the spinal column fractured and separated. That was the cause of death. The Coronet having summed up tn. evidence, the jury, after a few moments' deliberatisu, returned a ver- dict of " Accidental death."

div.head: OUTLINE OF TER STORY.
div.p: OUTLINE OF TER STORY.

MR JOSEPH Hommel. has chosen a great theme for his latest novel, and the widespread interest aroused by the dissensions in the Church of England makes it certain that his tale will be eagerly read and much discussed. Duncan Rut! md is the youthful minister of a flourishinz Nonconformist Chapel in a Lancuhire town. In the neighbourhood there is but one aristocratic family, known far and wide for its great tra itions, and its fealty to the Roman Catholic faith. Duncan imperceptibly falls in love with the daughter of the house. She is repelled by his Pro- testan.tista and by the fact that he is winning numerous converts to the Pr,t,stant faith. At first she seeks to discredit him In the town by inducing Father Sheen, her confessor, to meet Duncan in public controversy, but Father Sheen is badly worsted and a dastardly attack upon Duncan by a gang of roughs whom she had unwittingly incited is foiled by the heroine herself.

Father Sheen, demoralised by defeat, calls in the aid of the celebrated Jesuit Father Ritzoom. It is then and there determined to undermine Duncan's faith by means of h.s love. Every force that wealth and culture and noble traditions can cem nand is brought to bear upon Duncan, who is emiced to Rome with his sweetheart, where Nis final tempta- tion takes place. This terrible inward struggle. growing in intensity as time advances and as the fascinations of spiritual Rome unfold themselves, is admirably portrayed.ang the breathlessly interesting climax will enchain the attention of every reader.
JOSEPH HOCKING'S NEW STORY
IN THE
" EXAMINER,"
JUNE 15TH.

THE burden of British Is the Orb of Fate Too Vast? Empire was described mall

years ago as a too vast orb of Fate. It has wonderfully increased since then, as the result of many agencies. Consider what these agencies are. The most specific of men have always had an interest in suppressing the slave- trade, and we have spent millions of money in catching slave-vessels, in preventing the organised march of slave-gangs trona the ieterior of Africa to the slave-markets, in reconstructing small States, where slavery has been paramount, and in appoint- ing governors and officials whose business it mainly was to carry out our beneficent aims. Our Im- perial responsibilities have been increased,dieeetly and indirectly, as the result of this humane, and at one time almost exclusively British, crusade. The extension of missions has been another factor of Empire. Where the missionary has gone the trader has followed, and also the soldier. Cruel sarcasms have been expended on this system of extension. But what Government has had . the audacity to forbid missionaries because there was danger? It was the danger that was the inspira- tion. Khartoum is perhaps the principal instance in which the soldier has preceded the missionary. How is the Gospel to be preached to the heathen by staying at home ? The case of Uganda is a mixed one. Here commerce and Christianity were blended, and ultimately came the Imperial Government and the rail- way. In China the missionary has been in advance of the merchant, though in India the merchant cleared the ground for the missionary. The machine power of this country has made the el- , tension easier. Enterprising discoverers,inerchants ' and adventurers have built up Empire. The facts , are undoubted. The very men who dislike the word Imperialism also object, to a policy which would leave the missionary to his fate, and allow , the enslavement of the negro, and permit the savage to burn out the merchant or play the part of the pirate. We have to vindicate principles te assert oar strength, to maintain our authoritY• Of great longings for Empire, there are none. Mere pushing out into unknown regions, to in- -1 crease the territories under our rule, is a fiction of the brain. Events compel us. It isFate,says one ;it is Christian conquest,says another. The orb grows. Bat who ventures to say that we should cease our efforts to repress slavery, recall our missionaries ' and forbid our merchants seeking for new markets? There are wurnblings over the spirit of greed, of militarism, of Jingoism—and very healthy and tonicising they are, for the most part, as morel and intellectual exercise. But we cannot contract the British Empire as if it were a mere businese concern, and we could "cut a loss." Humaniti and honour forbid. And so the orb grows, and the weary Titan sometimes groans under his load. Still, he has to bear it, or to undergo moral and mental deterioration. There are two great duties, it seems to us, that the present position of the British Empire imposes—we are excluding South, Africa for the time being—we must develop go.' qualities at home,sobriety, citizenship, and libertf; we must carry into Imperial rule the high Chris.; tian qualities which have made a good deal. of 1 possible, and accept the fact that our mission in the world is not and cannot be limited to thil. British Isles. Contraction means decay quite e; I muck as undue expansion means weakness. Jhs now in China the British policy is to avert a.decl ' that would be a calamity to the world. It is PAlo for us to have a new burden thrust upon us, bui the kingdoms of the world are being reconstitute': and the Powers of the past find it difficult .ti, withstand the light, Lir and new ideas of the civlA ising spirit. If Englishmen are to keep ahead se' de to retain the virgin impulses which have 012 them pioneers, emancipators. and Christianisers/ the orb can never be too vast.

THE huge, unwielal The Breaking up in China. Empire of China seer danger of breaking There has been no more serious crisis then present one for many Tars. The dynastY liega always had some control when it desired exercise it, and unruly elements, though may have triumphed for a time, have been gene-t; ally put down. The present disturbances folio's/di curious phase in what it is almost an anachronise; as well as an anomaly to call the development new policy. China was to be opened to the in' 01 ences of Western progress. The horde of once sion-seekers at Pekin were treated with the res; pect that Chinese officials always shove to perseen out of whom money ia to be made., Some , sands of pounds have been expended in gift° erial considerations, and various railway, mining, 11-ot exploration concessions were given 0 0 t f reigners 101 all nationalities,as the result of many intriguee much competition. In an unlucky hour the Emperor conceived the idea of remodellieg er Government upon civilised ideas. The D°°94400 Empress at once reap) eared, and the fate ei e je Emperor waszesled. Where he is, whether to alive or Lot, no one can definitely say ; hll2 he the ceased to be an active personal force, en or. northern part of the country is under the tenir Pe r° sty control of fanatics, called Boxers, aloe • ner°' ifessed object is to rid the country of fereig whether they be missionaries or railway engillbeee: sTwo British missionaries are known to haYe Peens' murdered, and probably seine other Eure also French, Italians and Belgians, have b eelo killed. The centre of this reaction is te 0400 too bourhood of Tientsin. What makes the d athy trouble so daugerous is the gen)

plicity of the Dowager Empress and the relatives _of the Heir-Apparent. They are in league with the Boxers, and ivhen they order the suppression Of the secret society and send soldiers to put it clown they also issue secret instructions that the soldiers are not to fire upon the Boxers, who are tearing up railways, burning stations, and creating terror wherever they go. They are now threaten- ing Tientsin, and representatives of the European Powers have had to land sailors and marines to , Protect their interests at Tientsin and Pekin. Obstacles were offered to these measures of pre- Caution, but they have bean overcome. Now ccarues the biggest tangle of the whole problem. Can the Powers agree to act together and to put Pressure upon the Chinese Government? They IneY Protect their respective interests. But some- thing more than this may become imperative,and it Seetli3 to be in the minds of some of the Powers te do nothing likely to carry interference any further, whilst at least one of them is suspected of desire to hasten the time when China will pass eut of the control of the Chinese Government. ..ltussia is thought to be intent upon taking China .111 hand, because Pekin and the Northern Province iS her sphere of interest and influence, and she Woul4aot be averse to installing herself in the old "Pital as the saviour of the country. The present insurrection will be destructive of European establishments and properties. It will put back atairs for many years. Does it warrant, however, the extraordinary measures suggested? It is ex- tlntaely difficult to say. To protect a dynasty Which is in league with the anti-foreigner move- raent would seem to be absurd. To overturn it Would be a big undertaking. To replace it by a temporary military authority would hardly be less Stations. Lord SALISBURY'S views are unknown. He Will naturally prefer to keep in line with the other Powers, and as long as all are agreed, and acting In harmony, there would seem to be no serious danger. Whether they will continue to do so esunot be predicted with safety. Probably at the .Ist pinch, the Rnssian Government may suggest tkereic measures, and prepare to back them un by 4usaian soldiers A situation would then arise in /thleb Pekin would come nnrl e. Russian control.

They see so-called balance- eats published from time to time making it more Z.less clear that some cottager in a favoured dis- ti let earned so many shillings per hen—it is some- es• put as high as thirty—and the conclusion irresistiblethat with so many hundred hens 4;rY considerihla profits may be made. is•clgt 'l4" orkhouse Infirmary was opened with e‘itiarpst Thursday afternoon. The Board of 4aver,,,miarl4 were especially fortunate in being kid tied with the presence of Sir J. T. Hibbert tfor,,r' j• M. Rhodes, twa ardent and renowned Zkitilc„Za in Poor Law administration. Sir John ~whieC, 128 speech at the opening ceremony wa.s one b'lnPels thoughtful consideration. He touched %earl °Or Liw work .in many of its aspects and • (lemonstrated his complete mastery of the Some of the points raised were of a de- whilst others were of a reassuring ;,‘ pre.,7". There may be some for instance who • e;ellt are not disposed to agree with him that ;Ts r:.enditure of £35 000 upon a hospital for Zts Poor is one of the best investments :m„lgliCh'ePrayers ever made. Then again, others I,ls‘ th„2"ound who no not entertain his fears that s'ttiv.CO. Prosperous times the people who are -16 large wages are not laying by what 6EI

ought to do for a rainy clay. This is not the time to take a pessimistic view of the thriftiness of the people of this country when the rapid and continued progress of thrift agencies is so marked. Curiously enough, Dr. Rhodes I gave an apt illustration on this very point at the dinner lseld later in the day. He stated that in 1850 there were one million depositors in the Sav- ings Banks whereas in 1900 the number had in- creased to ten millions. Such an increase in 50 years should at least inspire us with the hope that we may look forward to a still larger develop- ment in this direction as work and wages improve.

One of the most interesting passages in Sir John Hibbert's speech was his reference to the more humane treatment or paupers by the Guardians of the present day as compared with that of a quarter of a century ago. In this connection we believe that Warrington will compare favourably with most Unions. By th, introduction of the classifi- cation scheme in which Mr. A. J. Jolley has taken a leading part, and also by such a useful effort as the Brabazon Scheme much has been done to relieve the monotony and tedium endured by those who have unfortunately to spend their declining years in the Workhouse. The new infirmary is another step in the right direction. For a number of years, the Work- house Infirmary has been anything but a credit to us, but this reproach has now been effectively wiped out and we can point to the new buildings with a certain amount of pride. The only regret attaching to it is that such extens;ve buildings are striking ' evidence of a surprisingly large amount of suffering amongst the very poor of the town. In this con- nection it is well to bear in mind the weighty testi- mony of Dr. Rhodes who informed the company which afterwards assembled in the Lion Hotel, that the cause of much of the suffering amongst the poor was directly traceable to the insanitary dwellings in which they dwel. There were many members of the Town Council present and we hope they will take the hint.

A Provincial Letter.

Reports in the dsily papers from the various sea side places of public nsort 'lrwin.' the cost on the prospects of the summer season are mostly uf an encouraging and favourable character. But there ar6 one or two of them suggestive of a prebable slight falling off in the number of pleasure seekers, consequent upon the extra demands made upon the public purse by the war and in other ways. In the yachting world a slump had become inevitable. The upper ranks of society have been hard hit; by the present campaign, and share in the desire for an early and a peaceful settlement, on a proper and substantial basis, at least as earnestly as those in the humbler walks of life. ~es regards certAn of the latter, those who have this week been doing " the grand tour were surprised to fief] that the railway companies at short notice, if any, had abandoned the v-Ty convenient system a 'opted last year of collecting end delivering lugg ige at a cherge of "the nimble sixpence " per pikl.4e, and had actually doubled the fee. The experiment appears to have succeeded too well during the time it wa- in operation,and to have quite ups'-t the companies' calculations. But a hundred per cent. in Tease! This proved too much for the thrifty paterfa nilias and his family ti bear without grumbling, and grumb!e they did, but, of coarse, paid. If the com- panies would consilerately split the difference by substituting the nimble ninepence for the shilling now exacted, the change would still be regaried as a bOOR, ani be appreciated, but the shilling makes it now seem a tar.

; Whitsuntide has always been regarded as the seascn for the great Friendly Society gatherings. When the Societies were yet young the members annually walked in procession through the streets to attend Divine Service, held their annual feast, a nd,in parts of Lancashire and Yorkshire especially these wholesome and p'cturesque practic -s have been strictly olerved during the present week. But nowadays also. elected reresentatives attend the annual session of what are fitly termed the Par- liaments of their respective Orders, to review the acts of their executives, and mike the laws whieh govern the branches,of their different organizations. Thus the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows assembled at Portsmouth, the National Order of Odifellows met at Mancheeter, and the Ancient Order of Shea- herds journeyed to Bristol. on Monday, while on the following day the annual se4sion of the Gran.l United Order of Odd fellows was op.nel at Crewe, and Druids, Free Gar leners, Shepherds,and Romans have during the week met in other parts of the country. These Societies admittedly exercise an immense amount of influence for good all over the country, and the doings of the "delegates " are watched through the newßpaper reporte, with en equal amount of iaterest by individual members everywhere, who, on these occasions stein a po.i- tion to draw comparisons between their own and kindred societies, as well as to keep an eye upon their appointed representatives. Although Whitsuntide prospects were not at all bright and encouraging at the end of last week, Whitsuntide weather proved al !nest everything that could be desired by the not ton exacting' B iokinga for going away were declared to have been fewer on Saturday than had been known in London for a quarter of a century. This appeared hard to beli ye in the provinces, particularly at the health resorts on Monday and Tuesday, but lately the war has, accounted for many thing, and this fallin--off in early bookings among the rest. With the wea• her, no fault could reasonably be found, and so the crowds of holiday makers appeared to believe and feel.

One of the ways in which the effects of the war have been generally felt is in the enhanced price of coal, and now it will extend, ir, appesre to gas. The beginning of July is the period in most cases for the renewal of contracts between the dispeusers of vess and the proprietors of coal, and already notices are appearing in tunny plaees of an intended increase of price for the former The look-out at present is not very promiiieg, the probable ending of the war netwithstend'ng. It is declared by those competent to give a trust- worthy opinion,that there is little likelihood of coal again falling to the figure at which jt Atoll a yelr or two ago. Probably we ehall have to pay increased prices for fuel, as not only have the rates of waczes increased—thoueli not to the extent that would warrant the preNent advance in charges to the con- sumer—but freight is higher, and in one way and another prices may be maintained, since dealers are not wanting in regard to excuses for keening up the prices when they are already high So long as trade is good this may be no obstacle to gAneral progress, and the latest Boer. of Trade returns show no decline in the trade of the ceuntry, but it has come to be regarded as a truism that depression invariably follows high coal rates, and that as a rule this is a netural process ; for industries which are not being csrried on at a large profit soon feel the pinch, and hese to be closed in consequence of the difficulty of procuring cheap fuel. This. of course, is apart from the ordinary and housewives' point of view, which is, after all, about as import- ant as any.

It may not be correct to say that the premature announcement of the fall of Pretoria last week pre- judicially influenced the recognition of the event, when it was officially confirmed on Tuesday last, but generally speaking, the capture was not made so much of as was the relief of Mafeking The cir- cumstances were sufficiently diff•-•rent, and the surroundings of the two place, Mafeking and Pre- toria, in some respects so dissimiliar, as to account for much. But Ist us hope that. there will be no- thing lacking in the general display of enthusiasm when the time comes for observing the definite, for- mal, and official proclamation of peace. That is what most of us are waiting for, and %bat no doub many (71! those who took some part in Tuesday and Wednesday's demonstrations thought it best to re- serve themselves for.

A travelled correspondent, writing on the one subject of the last six or seven months, the war, says, very pertinently, that it is hard for him to conclude other than if the Boers had seized Durhsn, as they hoped and expected from the first. France and Germany would semi have found pretext for recognising the Republics as belligerents, and a European war would have been quickly facilitat-d. We have, in truth, been fighting for the very exist- ence of the present and future British Empire. Arising partly out of Whitsuntide experiences at the seaside, a matter has been brought to light which may affect the comfort and convenience of lholiday-makers at any other season and at other ' places chan the one in question,which, so far as this paragraph is concerned, shall be nameless. It ap- pears that a certain pier company witich for years

This, of course, is resented by the average freedom-loving Briton, wrio not only exposes the company concerned, but gibbets it an rue papers, lest other companies enamoured ot the money-making idea may be teaapted to follow such odious example. That very agreeable and upright judge, 11r. Justice Backnill, is about to show us,or at any rate the favoured people of Malden and Cuddington, what he can do in a one hundred and fifty yards veterans' race for persons over forty, at the athle:ic sports, of the local Jubilee Club and Invitute, on Saturday, the 301 instant. The new Master of the Rolls wa, a great sprinter in his 'Varsity days, but nis sporting feats appear to have been equestrian rather than pedestrian hitherto. It is recalled. not unkindly,that at Epsom,vrhese he has a fine gallop- ing ground, while riding during the early part of the present year Sir Thomas catne a bad cropper at a fence; whilo last year he had such a fall at beatherkead that his horse had to be killed.

Nearly everybody takes ti.• holiday, and those few left to labour and to wait for their holidays at some ot ler period find the towt4 as dead as the proverbial door nail. On ['burs- day the town had resumed somewhat of its normal appearance, but as a tradesman remarked the shops might close tor the whole of the week for what business would be done. In tact the month after Whitsuntide is a time of stagnation.

Next week Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School celebrates its c-ntenary,and t;iere are to be dm ms- t-ations on a rather elaborate scale. There are pictures of Boer and narim. life, faithful representations of the last stand of Major WEson in tile Matabale campaign and the recent battle of E ands- laagte, and some id,a of the huge show may be obtained when we mention that there are about 500 whites and natives. The ridince of the Boers and natives is marvel- lous indeed, and the driving in Malay carts is something which it is impossible to deieribe,The military elephants which accompany th 3 1110 Kr are wonders of docility and trainine. The whole i; under the able direction of Mr. Frank Fillis, rho w&L known "Barnum" of SJuh Africa and Mr. J. Pitt Elardacre, than whom no ~tie is better Itnown in the North of Eland. div.head: RUNCORN- AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN- AND WIDNES.
PRIMITIVE METHODIST CAMP MEETING.

On Sunday afternoon a goodly number of the members of Greenway-road Primitive Methodist Chapel carried out their usual custom of marching through the streets singing hymns,and subsequently held a camp meeting on Runcorn Hill. The pro- ceedings were conducted by the Rev. W. Fidoe, and addresses were delivered by Messrs Hill and Peacock and others. The hill was visited by a large con- course ot people. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH CHOIR.

On Saturday evening last the members of this choir, met to do honour to one of their oldest mem- bers Xtr. William Roach—who had been a member of the choir for 37 years but ha l now taken up his abode in Fleetwood. Canon Wood (Vicar) presided and with a fitting speech presented Mr. Roach, on behalf of the members of the choir and congrega- tion, with a handsome marble timepiece and bronze ornaments to match.—Other eulogistic remarks, as to Mr. Roach's attachment to the choir were made by Niessre Imison, Littler, Audley and Johnson, the recipient responding in very suitable terms.

div.head: WHIT TUMIDLY EXCIJUSIONS.
div.p: WHIT TUMIDLY EXCIJUSIONS.

The bookings at Runcorn railway station show that the number of people who travelled in search of pleasure was about equal to previous years. Liverpool, of course, took tue lead with 1,800 and then came Trodsham 400, Chester 300, Belie Vae 200, and Blackpool 150. In addition to these 2850 persoas, the trip dowa the Saip Canal and Mersey to ti.:astham and Liverpool, promoted by the Mersey Nlission to Beamen was well patronised,7oo persons being aboard, as was a similar trip organised by the Weston Wesleyan Sunday school. With this large exodus of people and the closing of the shops Run- e )rn was extremely quiet and presented the appear- ance usual on Sundays.

div.head: HA.LTON AND THE INDIAN 11 AMINE FUND.
div.p: HA.LTON AND THE INDIAN 11 AMINE FUND.

About. nine o'clock on Wednesday the villagers of Halton turned out en masse and formed into proces- sion at the Square. Headed by a "Hooligan Band," and nondescript characters, the boys brigade, and the church lads brigades, augmented by an Ama- zon Brigade of young girls, paraded the principal streets with " Kruger (Hr A Rowe), and " Mrs Kruger "(Mr Joseph Astbury, jun.), and two other prominent Boer characters as prisoners. Four pretty young girls Misses A (Ctssie) Howard, Nellie Looker, Phoebe Barrow, and Marjory Faulkner dressed as nurses, acted as collectors and succeeded in getting 233 which was handed over to the locil fund in aid of the Indian Famine Relief. Tee pro cession was altogether a very imposing one, and the costumes under the torch and lantern ligats looked exceedingly unique. When near the gas- works Krug.-r condeScensied to address his visit ors, and admitted that had he known auy of the Halton Boys' Brigade were coming out against him be would have surrendered long ago.

The Melice! Officer reported that the number of deaths registered during tee month amounted to 26 ; one was an inquest case, and the remaining 25 deaths were attributable to the folio whs. causes :—seven were due to pneumonia, two tI erten it degeneration, two to bronchitis, two te phthieis. tvel to thbility, and one each to other diseases. The 26 id,a•Als showed an average of 16 4 per thousand of the estiue ed population; and exclusive of the inquest case ot 15 7 Forty-seven ter hs were registered ane for the cerresnmding in mth of last yen', 30 deathi, and 51. b r h 3 weir,: registered. Tee Chairman observed considering the state of the atmosphere, and how hot it had ben, the report was very satisfactory. There did not appear to be any death due to intectious disewees during the moith. Dr. McDeugael veld he wi-trid to call attention to the practice of fish dealers and fruit dealers sto:ing trade refuse in the rz.ar of their premises. A case hid come under his notice during the last few days which he felt called upon to take notice of as a very serious offence, as he considered it was a case of gross neglect. It would appear obvious to the authority that it was practically a matter of implssibility to keep down the death rate if people were allowed te accumulate such refuse at the backs of their shops, especially seeing that the stuff could be removed at so little cost to them. Nor was it a matter of danger to the people who committed such acts aloue, but the immediate neighbours, who were entirely innocent, had to sutler most seriously. De wished to issue the warning that it would be his duty to advise the Council to take extreme drastic measures in all snub cases. At the same time it was a matter of congratulation that the town was free from infectious disease during the hot weather, but unless steps were taken to abate the dangers he referred to they might be called upon to suffer from diseases which were not of an infectious character. He had advised Mr Marshall of the case and it would come before them in due course.
The Chairman said the Council were much obl7„ed to Dr ideDougall for his observations, alai as lit as they could they would support him. ([Tear, hear.)

div.p: WHITSUNTIDE
Processions at Runcorn.

The Whteuntiee heiidays commenced at Runcorn on Saturday and most of the works were closed until Thurs- day morning With the exeeption of a few hours on Monday Meroine the tridessnen closed their shops for •be first Urea days of the week. It is some years since Whitsuntide has been savoured with such glorious weather. Bright sunlight and balmy breezes were the prevailing features although 'I uesday was somewhat dull. N -ver hat Rune mn preaentnl a brighter aspect then it did on Menday and the streets were thronged with people from early morn until late at night. Mr. Pr solicitor, defended on behalf of Mr Joseph 13it8rstto°"' 0. solicitor, Runcora.—From the evidence it appeared that the four m2n were enjoying themselves at Overton, and agreed to walk to Frodsham together. On the way an old quarr4 ot. aboat two years standing was reopened, and toe men set to and fought. In the course of the fight Queenan was injured sustaining a severe Pound in the neck, and also one in the cheek. No medical evidence was given, but one of the witnesses stated Oast a doctor had given it as his opinion that the wound in the neck was ms'.; likely caused by some blunt instrument. It wee dangerous, and the jugular vein had been narrowly miss-d. It was also alleged that the wound in the cheek was caused by a bite.—Francis Flynn was fined 20s and 11 6 i costs. and Richard Flynn fined lOs and costs lls 6,1, both 13;ing bound over for eix months to keep the peace.

When the boys came out of the circus, Beckett went to William Lucock and de- manded to have his share of the shilling as previously agreed Both the Lucock's demurred and Beekett began to be aggressive. He attacked William Lucook and prisoner interfered to defend his brother. Beckett then attacked the prisoner and somewhat severely handled him. The brothers then went away towards the end of Bewsey-roai and they were again overtaken by Beckett who shouted " Where's that monkey Fred." He at once rushed at the prisoner, butted him in the head and otherwise assaulted cim. The stone struck the boy on the head and he fell to the vround. He was taken to the Infirmary, and it was found that be had sustained a fractured skull. He was an inmate of the loititutioa for severe' weeks. Lncoek was after- wards apprehended by the police, and when charged he replied .• Yes, but he started of me first." He (the Chief Constable) bad every reason to believe that the facts as he had stated them were absolutely correct. rhat was the version of he affair as given both by the prisoner and prosecuter. SHOCKING ILLTREATMENT OF A FARMER'S WIFE At. too Warr,,glo., iloauty Petty Sessious on Wednes- day m rng bdore Mr. C. Morris (in ,he chair) ani Mr. J. Ball,James DaKon,formerly of Orchard Fartn,Cialchith, wassurnmoued for persi,tent cruelty to his wife,Eliz bth Daxon, whereby she h,d taqin compelled to leave him and live apart frina hon. —Mr Browne applared for ti-,e compla,nant, and tn. defendant was represented by Mr W Knowles—Mr B. owne said this was as bid a ca,,e as h had ever been his lit to appear in. The proneedings were .;aken under the Married Women's Act,1895,5, cion four of woich stated that a married woman whose husband hid been guilty of pe.rsistent cruelty such as caused hi r to leave him and live ap:rt, was entitled to a judicial s-paratiora and alimony in accordance ~tith the cireuinstarces. The parties were married at Christina,, 1893, and for some time they lived h ippity together. Du in., the la 4 few vears, howev r. his cruelty towards her ha.l been tereb`e. Ati-nit four ye +Fs ago h, illtrea.ted her, and she had ta go to the Liverpool Infirmary with a fractured finger. He r-fused to allow 11-r to go as oft. n as was necessary, with the result, that her arm grew to her side and she was oblgecl to g to a Manchi-s-er doctor, who had to tear the arm lion her body. She underwent great p tin. During the last SIX months he had us, d her yr•ry badly. Ele had continuady pulled her out of brd. 0 Sunday,the 18 h ult., she was in bed with indite; za. Us came home clruk, bringing with him t ;co other men He went up to his wife an./ insistfd on her getting up to supply tnem with ,lrink and something to eat. She went (lowa, but one of toe , men, seeing her canditiin.toll her to go bark to tied. On another night ho brought aMr and Mrs. Monks to the house,and in th-ir presence thumped his wife. S.ie and Mrs. Monks left the house, and where they re urned he picket up a piker, and told his wife that she had bitter say her pravers,f tr he was going to do it now. Re would have done it long since, he said, but for tiv children He further ad..ed that he had only to di- once. He then struck at her, and she managed to hold the piker and escape from the house. San stayed out all night. On one occasion he brought two men to the house at night, and when she complained he took up a cleaver and holding her apinst the wall, would, she blieve, have done her some bodily injury had not tie men int-rfered. On Sunday week he used such threat i to her :hat she left bim. He was formerly a farmer ...nd was sold up about a c wple of months ago.—Complainant asked for rra,onable alimony.—Complainant gave evidence in supp qt of Mr, Browne's statement. She said she was afraid to live with the delendant, and a.•=ked for a judicial s, paration and reasonable alimony. Defendant'm idea in s-i ing toe farm was to start as a contractor. When she left him he had two donkeys, three ponies and two horses, a waegonette. two traps, and two tubs Since he sold the farm he had been drinking heavily.—Mr. Knowles said it would not be necessary to call further evidence. He would not say that the wife was not entitled t.) a s-p4ra- don order, hut with regard to alimony he would Point out that all defendant had in the world wal a stock-in- tr ide wrrth about £5O. He was past work, and would probably be ia the workhouse in twelve months' time. It was as much as he could do to keep himself The complainant bad arm. means and was able to work. • suggested an order ot 2s a week. Defendant had now sizned the pledge, and he (Sir. Knowles) hoped he would keep it.—The magistrates granted a judicial separation order, and ordered a payment for maintenance of 51 a week.

A MOTHER'S BAD ExAMPLES—WHOLERALE POCKET PICKING BY A LITTLE GIRL. At the Warrineton Boroulta Police Court on Werinee- day, Martha azebeth Barker, 10 years of age, was charged with sealing from the pereon of Annie D meld- son, whilst standing on the Fair Ground,Q.reen-street at 745 on Wednesday May 9th, a purse containing 14s ; also with stealing a purse containing 25; and a ewe-el order for 51 he property of Elizabeth Cliffs on Mw 13 h and with etealing trnm he person of Mary Ellen M ,Iy- neux whilst standing in Church-street a purse containing 9; —She pleaded guilty to each charge. The Chief Con- stable said that was one of the most extraordinary cases tbat was ever brought before the Becch.The prisoner v 7 -re only ten years of age and lived with her parents in Dial- street. For some months pest there had been a regular system of picking pockets on market days and he and Superintendent Monaghan had worked hard to detec, the culprits but in vain. However, on Tuesday morning the little girl's mether was before the court on a Charaeo of bine, drunk and disorderly and was committed to prison for a month. Certain informatien thee came to the knowledge of himself and S neerintendent Monaghan and the girl was arrested. As regarded the first charge it appeared that Mrs Davidson, who resided in Foster- street was standieg on the fair ground and felt a hand in her pocket. She turned round and saw the prisoner making away amongst the crowd. On putting her hand in her pocket she found the purse was gone. She followed the girl into Queen-street and accused her. She indignantly denied havine stolen the purse but Mrs. Davidson lifted up her ' apron and found the purse containing 14.1 in her hand. She took it from her but unfortunately allowed her to go. It appeared that the prisoner was accompanied on almost every occasion when she committed thefts by a little girl named Clare who, however, did not take any part in them and did not reap any benefit. As regarded the second case, Mrs. ClitTe was standing in Mere" -et., at three o'clock on the afternoon of Sunday the 13-h of May watchingt the Trades' Union;sts proces.ion. She had in her pocket a purse containing 25; and a pos,al order. She subeequeatly missed the purse and gave infermation to the police. Prisoner admitted stealing it and it appeared that she was accompanied by the girt Clare on that occasion. She was further charged with stealing a puree containing 9; from the per-on of Mary Ellen Molyneux on the 27th of May. Prosecu- tor was standing in Church-stoet watching the Volun- teer church parade and the theft was committed in a similar manner to the previous ones. He (Mr. Talbot) had a list of thirty cases of pocket pieking in the market alone during the last few months and the amount stolen totalled to about £3O 103. The peliee had reason to believe that the prisoner and her mother were the culprits in the cases. He asked that the girl might be sent to a reformatory. She had been taught to pick pecketa by her mother who was an expert and had been convicted several times. The girl had no doubt been contributing largely to the maintenance of the family by that perch- clone practice. A. puree was found in her pissession when arrested, and she admitted styling it from the pocket of some unklown woman in the Market Place. She had said that her mother often burnt the purses. It was his intention to proceed against the woman for re- ceiving stolen pods on her release from gaol.—The Bench decided to send the girl to Mount Vernon Green Reformatory for five years.—The police would be glad if any person who lost a puree on Saturday last in or about the market would communicate with the Chief Constable or Superinten ant Monaghan.

EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF DESERTION—A CRIMINAL'S STRANGE CAREER Oa Saturday, at the Warrin ston Police Court before Messrs J W Hayward (chairman) an I It T Fairclough, young man named Mathias Pye w, a charged with being a deserter from tne des.ô-. of the Lancashire Fast- tiers, stationed at Bury since the 2ad ~f January.—P.C. Lewis stated that at 4.45 hat morning he was an duty in Dallam-lane and met the pri-ooer. Immediately he saw him he ran away and witness, becoming suspicious followed. He succeeded in capturing the man and questioned Wu- as to nis whereabouts. He did not give any satisfactory answer and wit- ness remembsred sometime ago seeing a report in the newspapers that a mar, answering the prisoner's description was arrested at N irth mien for de- serting. He told prisoner this but ne denied it. He took him to the Police Station and Inspector Rowb Atom telephoned to Norrhwich and ascertained that prisoner was arrested thtire in November for deserting from the Lancashire Fusiliers and was remanded to await escort. Prisoner now admitted that he had deserted from several other regiments.—The Chief Corstatee said it was an extraordinary case. Prisoner was a most persistent young criminal having been before the court three times for deserting. He said that he desert d from the Lanca- shire Fusiliers at. Bury, in January. He then j.l ed toe Kings Royal Rifles, and eeserted from the regiment at Gosport in March, and j tined the Royal Field Artillery. He broke out of the cells at the Barracks on " Mat king night" and enlisted in the Liverpool Regiment at New- port. To his astoniahment and no doubt consternation he was sent to Warrington and he was wandering about the streets when met by P.C. Levi. He was altogether incorrigibl., When arrested he had in his possession a large bunch of keys two of which were skeleton keys.— Prisoner was remanded to await e-cort. A GRAVE BREACH OF TRUST.—CURIOII3 CASE. At the Warrington Police Curt, on Monday, before Mr. F. Monks (in the chair) and other magistrates, William Bolton, 7, Water-stree, L itchford, a, as charged with stealing from outside the shoo eif J. N. Brown and Company, 162, Bridge-street, at 10-15 on Saturday even- ing, a pair ot boots, value 53 6 I.—Tne Chief Constable said that Messrs. Brown, in common with m,st boot dealers, expesed boo's for sale eursioe the shop, but they took some precautions to see that the public sere not tempted to steal them. The prisoner was engaged to stand outside and wWch the boots, and be had been employed for that purpose for some considerable time. Recently the suspicions of the manager had been excited, and on Saturday night he cans d the errand boy to le Op a close watch on the prisoner. At the time in question the bey sa,w him walking atone in front of the shop and brushing against the boots with his shoulder. He then snatched a pair of boots, put them under his coat and bolted round the corner into Friars'-gate The manager pursued him and eventually caught him. He accused the man of stealing the boots and he denied having done so, Be was searched but the boots were not found in his pos- session. Ultimately they were found in a beck passage in the vicinity. Prisoner wag taken to the Police Station and when charged he at first denied all knowledge of the theft. He now said he took them whilst under the in- fluence of drink. Be had beet, before the Court 14 times.—Prisoner said he remembered nothing at all about the theft. He was in a state of intoxication.— P.C. Reddington was called and stated that when arrestel the prisoner ayes not drunk and knew what he was doing.—The Bench considered the ease to be a very grave breach of trust and committed prisoner to gaol for a month with hard labour.

JULIA'S JUBILEE* Julia Ann Shields, a well-known etarart ir to the police, appealed at the Warrinetou Police Court on Mon- day on a charge of being drunk and disorderly in Dial- street at 7.50, the p evious night, and with assaulting Constable Clough—The officer stated that at the time in question he was on duty in Dial-street and heard the prisoner, who was very drur.k making use of filthy language towards her mother. She went into the Raven Hotel and asked to be supplied with beer but the landlord refused to serve her. She came into the street again and used disgusting language. He requested her to go home but she refused and he was obliged to take her into cured?. She became very violent, threw hereelf to the ground. and tore all the clothing off her holy. Wittres c tiled upon a young man to as-let hirn.and with great difficulty they got tee prisoner to the Police Statioe.—On arrival there she struek him a violent teller an the face.—The Chief Constab,o otti i that the prisoner was an easy first amongst teeir incorrigibles Tnat was her 50:h appear- ance so that she celebrated her jubilee in that court.— She was committed to gaol for a month with hard labour for being drunk and disorderly, and three months for the assault (four months in all). SHOCKING CRUELTY T 1 A DOG. At the Warring, n Police Court on Tuesday. before Mr. John White and Alderman Sutton, Michael O'Neil, a young man, was charged with cruelly illtreating a dog on the 26th of May.—Cetha.rine O'Neil, the defendant's mother stated that at 8 o'clock on the date in question defendant came home under the influence of drink. He pickEd up the dog and dashed it to the floor rendering it unable to stand. The animal was taken to the Police Station and it wee found that one of its legs was broken. It was afterwards destroyEd by the police.—E -1 ward O'Neil. defendartt's brother saw defendant pick up the dog by the shauldeis, squeere its neck end throw it on the floor breaking ite leg.—P.C. Cooper (20) said that at 3 p.m. on the date in question he was on duty at the Police Station when the &fondant's mother came in. In consequence of whit she told him he prozeeded to Fen- nel-street and saw defendant's brather carrying a smooth haired terrier dog. One of ti tore legs was very badly broken and the animal's shoulders seemed to have been in- jured. It appeared to be in very great pain and was howl- ing. Inspector Phillips °Tiered him to destroy the doe.— Inspector Brown s tid he saw thedefendant later on and the only excuse he could give for his conduct was that he was mad drunk.—DPFebdant, who made his fourth appearance was fined 104 and costs (£1 fis in all) with the alternative of 14 days' imprisonment. MORE TEMPTS FRold TEE MARKET. GLIB AND FLUENT LYING. Edith Iligginson, 32, Melville street. appeared at the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, on a charge of stealing from the stall of Emily Townsend in the Market Place at 4 o'clock the previous afternoon, A pair Of lady's kid gloves and a silk handkerchief value 3s 5d and also of stealing from the stall of Thomas Edward Leigh at 2.30 the same afternoon a white table cloth value 4s.— She pleaded guilty.— fhe Chief Constable related the facts of the eas from which it appeared that P.C.'s Clarke and Monks were on duty in the Market Place in Wain clothes in consequence of complaints of thefts and pilfering and observed :he woman at Mrs Townsend's ,stall acting in a very suspicious manner. They saw her take up a pair of kid gloves, conceal them and walk away. She walked round the Market and then bad the audacity to come back to the stall and buy Isome lace. Whilst the assistant's back was turned she picked up a ails handkerchief, concealed it and a yain walked away. The officers stopped her and in her pos- session was found the table cloth mentioned in the second portion of the charge. She was taken to the Police Station and lied glibly and fluently about the whole thing. She now, however, pleaded guilty. Prisoner was a married woman and had absolutely no reason fir committing the thefts. She bad not been before the Court previously. The matter was becoming a public scandal.—Taking into consideration that the woman had not miaconducted berself previously the magistrates impofed a penalty of 20s including costs, with the alternative of 14 days' irnprisenment.—The money was paid.

div.head: STRIKE OF JOINERS AT
div.p: STRIKE OF JOINERS AT
WARRINGTON.

On Thursday last week, about 100 joiners in War- rington ceased work. The reason of thi4 is a dis- pute with the masters as to the rate of wages and other matter Q affecting the trai!e. We unders%and that in December last, the joiners affiliated with the Union, made a request to the master builders of Warrington for an advance of wages per hour, a reduction in the number of apprentices and a revision of the working hours, to take effect on the first of June. Since the notice was sent several conferences have been held be- ten representatives of the Builders' Association and the men, but as no satisfactory arrangement had been come to at the time of the expiration of the notice, the men ceased work at tl,e builders shops and also at a number of private firms in the town.

_ A conference of mAsters and the men's repreeen- tatives was held on Friday night,but nothing &finite has agreed upon. It is believed to-at a further at- tempt to settle the matter will be made at an early date

WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE FEDERATION.
Annual Meeting.

The anaual meeting of the Warrington Temperance Federation was held in tne Florsemarket-ureet• Cocoa Rooms on Thursday last week, Councillor Luke Ellison presiding. Mr. William Roberts, the hoc). t:ecretary, presented the report and balance sheet for the year juA closed.
THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JUNE 8, 1900

div.head: SECRETARY'S REPORT AND BALANCE SHEET.
div.p: SECRETARY'S REPORT AND BALANCE SHEET.

The report was as follows :—" Your Committee has much pleasure in again presenting its annual report. The work of the Federation during the past year has not ben so vieerous as in former years, owing to the fact that your Committee has been most anxious to give the Warrington Band of Hope Union the fullest opportunity of developing its organization so as to strengthen the various Bands of Hope affiliated with the Union. The earnest desire of your Committee is to help, and not to hinder, this valuable ally in Temperance work. It is very desirable, however, that whilst main- taining a separate society for adult work it should be remembered that as the Band of Hope Union confines its efforts to training the young in temperance principles it is advisable in the interest of both the Temperance Federation and Band of Hope Union that some aereement is necessary, so as to ensure united action in order to voice the temperance sentiment of the whole town when occasion demands. Your committee is greatly indebted to the choir of the Baud of Hope Union fr the valuable assistance rendered to the Federation at its meetings in Parr Hall and elsewhere and as a slight appreciation of this kindly help has voted a con- tribution to its funds. Your committee has also assisted t'n local brench of the British Women's Temperance Association in helping to arrange several public meetings end also in defraying a share of the expenses incurred. The work of the Police Court Mission so faithfully and successfully carried on by our friend Mr H Taylor, has again been supported by a contribution from our funds. The Federation has held two large meetings in Parr Hall dering the past year both of which were very successful. Your committee at the last Brewster Sessions and also the adjourned Sessions made an earnest protest against the rebuilciirg of the Feathers Hotel in Bridge Street but all to no purpose. The majority of the Town Council and magistrates seemed determined not to sacrifice the license and to have the new hotel built upon the old site. We greatly deplore their decision and c msider it a mistake acid a splendid opportunity missed of reducing the number of licensed houses in one of our principle streets where there are already six fully licensed heuses within a radius of one hundred yards. Your Committee cannot close this report without according its hearty cengratulations to Alderman H. Roberts. J.P., upon his unanimeus electien to the Mayoralty of War- rington. in N vember last. Thi3 appointment to the Chief Magistracy has given intense pleasure to all friends of the temperance cause ad we are satisfied that the best interests of the town will be fully maintained. Members of the committee have attended many meet- ings in various parts of the town during the winter and addressed large and appreciative audiences. The Federation will gladly supple epeakere free of expense to all affiliated societiee. Your Committee urge upon all who approve of Tenwrancs Legist aim, to strongly support the Sunday Closing Bill for Monrnouthshire,and the Bill for the Prevention of the Sale of Drink-to children Both these measures have already passed the second reading in the House of Commons, and it is to be hoped will be passed by the Legislature during the present Session. In conclusion yeur committee is thankful for the assistance given to the Federation in the past, and appeals to all friends of the movrment,to join its ranks and thus increase its usefulness for good. The work of spreading our principles is werthy of our best effort and the satisfaction of doing good will be our reward. The balance sheet showed the receints for the year to be £57 14; 111. the expenditure.£49 103,and the balance in hand. £8 43 91. The report aid balance sheet were unanimously adopted.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. Mishap to the Duke of . Norfolk. A Dislocated Hip.

The following has been po..,t?d at the War Office : —Lord Roberts reports that during the operations before Pretoria the Duke of nrfolk, Imperial Yeo- manry, had his right hip dislocated through his horse falling. Fortunately a doctor was on the field, who reduced the dislontion, and the Duke is now progressing satisfactorily.
Reported Boer Stand at Hatherley.
British Prisoners Removed to an Unhealthy Quarter.

A Renter's telegram, dated Lourenco Marques, June 7, says :—lt is reported that the Boers are making a stand near Hatherley, about twelve miles east of Pretoria for the purpose of gaining time. They are removing British prisoners to Nooitgedacht in the Zlands Valley, a most unhealthy spot. 300 prisoners arrived there on Tuesday, and 700 yester- day. A force of 250 Boers is guarding the prisoners there at present.

div.head: Captured Yeomanry.
div.p: The Captured Yeomanry.
Number of Casualties.

Our London correspondent learns upon inquiry at the Imperial Yeomanry offices that 14 officers and men of the 13th Battalion were killed,ineluding Captain Keith and Sir John Power, and 28 were wounded, including Lord Longford. All the rest are prisoners.

div.head: Colonel Ireland Blackburne.
div.p: Colonel Ireland Blackburne.

Mrs. Ireland Blackburne, writing to thank Miss Boylt for a further consignment of comforts for the militia battalion of the South Lancashire RegimPnt, says she still coatinues to hear that Colonel Blackbu:ne is doing well.

div.head: Trooper Broadbent's Experiences.
div.p: Trooper Broadbent's Experiences.

The following are extracts from further letters which have been re-eived from Trooper J. Broaqbe,t, who is serving with the Cheshire Yeomanry :—Kopje near Koega's Pant, Griqua:and, May 11th. We are all very well in spite of the cold, and enjoy it all right. We have been very short of food, but now have strict rations daily, 115 meat,lll3 biscuits, boiled mutton every day for dinner, coffee for breakfast.tea in the afternoon and anything else we can get when the cart comes from the store. The other day we bought a lot of golden syrup, potted meat, &c., and the same day C. B. received some tobacco and generously gave me a pound, se I am all right for the present. I have not received any sent from home yet. I have got two parcels containing socks. Tnev are the greatest possible comfort, and make me feel 1:11e a new man. This is a fine, healthy life,and in many ways it is a bitter experience to come as a trooper. It does do fellows a lot of good and thickens them out. Almost all look the better for the plain food, open air, Szc. I really never felt better in my life. It is very cold at night, but I enjoy sitting round the camp fire awfully. Curi- ously enough, it is colder sleeping under th trees by the river than it is on the kwjes, suppose it is the damp from the river. We spend most days in building forts on the kopks, which is heavy work, and we look like a lot of quarrymen. I wish we were with a big column now. It was grand when we were with Kitahener, and one felt such confideeca in one's general. Kitchener is a wonderful chap and one feels his influence although one does not often see him. lhere is an old man in Omen's Horse, about 70 called" Dad " with white hair and moustache which he dyed when he enlisted ! La.t night two of Omen's etarted at eight to have a look at the laager, walking all night andpiding at daybreak. This morning we heard a lot of shooting, so all went out and met these men coming in. They had fired on the Boer patrol and then returned home. There were 19 Been mounted. We were all on foot. When we were coining back they opened fire again, and we took up a position on a kcpje for some time till it stopped. I fully expect the rebels round here will disperse. I don't think they will attack here again, and they will be in a trap when a column marches through. I should like to have another smack at them.

div.head: With the Welsh Fusiliers. Letter from Private J. Massey.
div.p: With the Welsh Fusiliers. Letter from Private J. Massey.

Mr. Peter Pownall, of Warrineton•road, Fenketh, has received the following letter from Mr. J. Massey, his fellow workman, who, previous to going to the front, worked at Mr. W. D. Houghton's wire works, Sankey Bridges :—" Fourteen Streanee, May 9th, 1900. We lett Bronfield on the Ist of May, and marched to Windsorton Road Station, about 19 miles, where we bivoutcked with blanket and waterproof sheet, having left our tents behind. We stayed there till the 4th, marching out again in a westerly direction, doine a good day's march and tamping on the banks of the Vaal River close to the Windsorton Diamond Mines, which are reputed to pro- duce the finest emeralds in the world. But I did not find any. We started out again on the 15;h, having to ford the river, which was full of large pieces of rock. I am sure we must have looked a comical sight in going ever, some of the men stumbling against stones.and going in head first, causing roars of laughter; hut we managed to gat across without any serious accident. After drying and dressing on the other side, we again started march- ing, going through the town of Windsorean. After pro- ceeding about five miles we heard the artillery firing, sad then we knew that the enemy were not far away. Ws got into action abeut ten o'clock in the morning. There were the 4th regiments of the Union Brigade,three batteries field artillery, two Maxim-Nordenfeldta. and the Imperial Light Horse. We were soon in the firing line, and kept on a steady advance, firing at intervale —with the artillery behind thundering their shrapnel shells over our heads. As we got closer, the Mauser ballets of the Boers rained thicker around Us, and many of our fellows got knocked over,one man being wounded in no less than five places. When about a hundred yards off the Boer trenches we got the order to fix baycnets and charge, which we did, the Bone going on their knees and begging us to spare them. We took a lot of prisoners, and their dead and wounded were lying all ever the place. Tracks of blood could be seen in many places where a wounded man had either walked or had been carried away. Our dead, and those who died of wounds up to the present in my regiment number nire. We have also got about 20 who got 'winged' in the arm or leg. They have all been sent to the hospital at Kimberley. My churn got killed. Ho first got bit in the foot, and in attempt- ing to rise had a bullet through the bead. We had one of our captains killed whilst leading on his men, and a sergeant was shot through the stomach, dying the 941199 night You will coo that I have been very fortunate in coming out without a scratch. Th 3 name of the place where the battle was fought was Rooidam. I hardly knew whether I have spelt it correctly or not. General Barton gave us great praise after the battle was won. He said we had werked eplendidly, and he was proud te have such a brave regiment as the Welsh Fusiliers in his brigade. The doctor and chaplain were busy all night at their tasks,otie burying the dead and the other attend- ing the wounded, but everything wee straight by the morning (Sunday), when we marched off again te Four- teen Streams. There was a little firirie.. oa the way, but nothing of consequence. The Boers are reported to be retiring fast, 90 I think the war will soon be over, I hope so, as lam fed up—eicommon terra used by the soldier when he has had enough of anything. N more at pro sent.—yeurs sincerely, J. MASSEY, 955, Private J• Massey. 8 Company Royal Welsh Fusiliers, S.A. Field Forces."
Interesting Letter from Captain Crosfield.

Mrs. Crosfield, of Walton Lea, has received a letter from Mr. George Crusfield, who sailed in the Canada, in April last, as capta'& the 77ch Company Imperial Yeomanry. In it the writer says .—" 11;1;y 12th, Satur- day, McKenzie warm, Maitland Camp, Capet,iwn, S. A. I am writing this on tny wooden saddle case inside my tent, by the light of a single candle, even thouqh it is only 5.30, so soon does it become dark here. First of all lec me describe our quartPra ; we are most comfortable, and are in the bt part of Mait- land Camp. There are 13 ten's per clmpany, thri e being hr officers, !.o I, es elretnandint! otrtr:er, g,t ous to myseit. The men are 12 in a tent and have a fair amount of rerun, as the tent; are 12 feet in diarretrr. I cm awfully glad I brought a bed (one of thole folding up ones weighing 15Ib ), as it is most clmforiable. Of course one will not be allowed to take it up to the front unless one knocks off 15th out of the 35b. allowed, but while one is in camp here it is a Godsend, as Ova ground is distinctly hard. I have got plenty of warm clothing ; in fact I am short of ntthing, and am very fit and well, as are the majority of my men. The scenery here is lovely, end reminas one very much of Switzerland. When I wake in the morning (reveille is at six) the sun is just catching a cluster of fir trees which I can roe through the op.ning of my tent; behind them rime s grand mountain that reminds one of the.

Sorapies in the Tyrol, and the air is fresh and fragrant. Alas ! In an hour's time the freahness and fragrance have dieappearee, %Lid innumerable flies spring up from everywht re to annoy one all day long. Well, as to our arrival. We did not clisemhaek till Saturday. After getting the majority of our baggage togeth-r and seeing it safely stowee in a erest van, rake I on to a traction, and sending an N.C.O. and tea men to see that nobody collared it on the way, we awaited orders to proceed. After hanging about a couple of hours or so we got these, and forthwith set out on our tramp of five mi;es ; took two hours over this, and had had quite ' enough of the road when we arrived. This you must remember, coming after three weeks of inactivity. We soon settled down to camp life. The first night we only had seven tents, an some- body had ' bagged ' our other five (we had 12 Oh the Canada), so I sent Pilkington with tan men to fled them first thing on Monday morning- He went beck to the decks and got six not belonging to us but to the base depot, so now we are in clover and have painted the • base depot' over and put 77th Co's instead. Oa Sunday we had church parade. Oa Monday we went to the kraals and drew 119 horses, all Hungarians, and wonderfully good horses on the whole ; each officer gets two, and I've got two that will do me very well. They are only 14h. 2, but are very sturdy. They have attached us to the 16thliattalion Imperial Yeomanry, under Colonel Rigby, but we hope on Wednesday to go up to Piquetsberg and join our battalion, which is the Bth, uncles Colonel Crawiey, and consists of the Duke cf Lancaster's own, the Westmorelands, and ourselees After that we await our orders. Si far we have done nothing but riding school to get these horses trained. None of them have ever been ridden le.fore, and are wonderfully traeab!e considering. The day's programme is briefly :—Reveille. 6 a.m. ; stables, 630 to 730 ; breakfast, 8 ; riding school (in the epee of COW s-), 9 to 11 ; stables. 11 to 12 ; lunch. 1 !•0::) 2 ; clean eaddlery,2 to 3 ; parade, 4to 5; stables, 5 to 6 ; tea. Up to to-day, the officers in this company mess.ei in a tin hut near at hand, where they 'grubbed' you for 61 per day, and very indifferent at that. So to-day we have started on our own hook, and it has been a great suc- cess. We have an empty eadele case as a table. We draw :;he same rations as the men, and supplement it with the potted meat, sardines, that Captain Hutchinson so awfully kindly sent to me at Trafford. We get coffee in the morning and tea in the evening anti buy anollinaris for lunch. Breakfast and dinner we have outside, but lunch we have to have in- side my tent on account of the flies. Th's afternoon we entertained three of the nurses who were on the Canada to tea in the tent. We had a great tee, the tea being made by one of our servants. The one nuisance about the jets is-paying the men. On Monday, for instance, I shall have to ride into Cspetown and get £3OO in gold and silver; and then making up pay lists is rather com- plicated and wearisome—otherwise, the work is ehsolutelystraieh•f -e•ward, and so far the responsibility has ht-en nil. Isn't Roberts doing splendidly ? Most peeple give the war another two or three weeks; I . hardly think so myself, as he has got the Vaal to cross.

div.head: FALL OF PRETORIA.
div.p: THE FALL OF PRETORIA.
The News in Warrington.

The news of the surrender of Pretoria did not occasion any demonstrations of great enthusiasm at Warrineton. Immediately on the reception of the intelligence a Union Jack was hoisted at the Town Hall, an I xamnle which was quickly foil )wed by the political clubs. There was, however, only a limited display of flags and bunting in the main streets. In some quartets of the town, house- holders bestow( d some attention on decoratiog their premises and flags bearing such words as" well done Bobs" and " Pretoria is ours" were to be seen. School children were released from school at an earlier hcur than usual and gave vent to their joy bv cheering. In the evening bands of fantastically attired youngsters paraded the stree's singing patriotic songs and the streets presented an animated appearance.

div.head: Rejoicings in Runcorn.
div.p: Rejoicings in Runcorn.

Mr. Mack. of Savages Bridle, first made the news known in Runcorn by tee blowing of Ws hooter, and some minutes later the whieles nf the works joined in the welcome "din." This was about one o'clock. There was however, little if any demonstration. Compared with Ladysmith and Mafeking the display was weak— characterleos. In the first place there were abc,ut 4,09 people absent on pleasure bent, and the starters o! nearly, the whole of the shops were up. There were Rome flags and bunting flying, as had been the case for Some days past,and a number of private houses put forth some token of rejoicing. In the eveaing toe younl- eters succeeded in extracting some fun from the event. i They marched through the town in bands, blowing toy trumpets and obtaining souods far from musical from various tin and iron utensils of domestic value. In some cases effigies were borne aloft. One young shaver was rigged up t represent Kruger, his flowing beard tieing of a very yellowish cast. Every few yards one of the band would fire a " cap " with his toy gun, Kruger would fall as though severely wounded, and forward would then come an ambulance man with a bottle small in size, but apparently containing a mixture of great potency, for with one application to his m9uch, tbe old man was on his feet again and ready for the next volley." These boys caused much amusement.

div.head: Rejoicings at Earlestown and Newton.
div.p: Rejoicings at Earlestown and Newton.

The news of the capture of Pretoria WaR received in Earlestown on Tuesday shortly before one o'clock and the inforrnatian spread like wildfire. Within a very short space of time flags and streamers were displayed, and the principal streets were gaily deeorated. Jost before two o'clock, Messrs Slee atd Co.'s buzz :r was set going and this eeenif d to upset everything. At two o'clock when all the buzzers blew for the men to neume werk there was a general air of indifference,end e ithout exception the various works had to be shut down. At the Viaduct Works, a large number of men went in probably about 600, whilst a big crowd remained outside. Those who went in might as well have stayed out, as instead of getting to work, they stood in a group singing, patriotic songs. A number organised a procession, but the appeerance of Mr. Emmett, the superintendent, put an end to this. He soon saw it was no use keeping the men in, and his permission for them to leave the works was received with cheers. They then left in a bedy,and joining those outside they formed in procession and marched ue the town singing patriotic she, and cheer- ing. The town afterwards calmed down, but in the evening about 3 o'clock, people began to muster on the Market Sqtiare,and a gigantic procession was son after- wards formed, and headed by the Viaduct Works bind, paraded the streets of the town. The streets were packed with people, but the police say their be- haviour was all that could be desired. At Newton the rejoicings, although on a smaller scale, were none the less enthusiastic. Work was suspended early in the afternoon at Messrs. McCorquodale's and Messrs Gilles- pie and Mason's works, and in the evening there was a torchlight procession, headed by the bugle bind of the local volunteers. When darkness set in there was a fire- work display at Mr R S-rave's, Newton Park, and at the Conservative Club, Earleptown, which were witnessed by large numbers of people. Early in the afternoon an attempt was made by the workmen.to bring the children out of the schools, bat the tcheo!mastees successfully resisted the attempt, and the children had perforce to contieue their studies.

div.head: Scenes at St. Helens.
div.p: Scenes at St. Helens.

The news of the fall of Pretoria cre.iated the greatest joy in tit. Helens. The buzvr at Hardibaw Brook Chemical Worki, immediately on receipt of the irtte;li- aence soundrd loud and lona, and soon aftQr othei• buzzers joined in. The roadway at Peaaley Cross and the main streets of the town were quickly fill:2cl with people. The school children paraded the street!' in fan- tastic co,durnes, and the scene throughout the town was a most animated one.
Ohmy's Circus.

This week Mr. Ohmy brings to a close his short but successful visit to Warrington. During his stay in the town his reputation as an amusement caterer has been enhanced, and the circus hos been patron- ized by large audiences. The past week has been no exception to the rule in this respect, and those who have visited the Queen-street Louse have been amply repaid for doing so. The chief attrac- tion is the military spectacle "To Pretoria " which is presented by 100 local children. The performers are highly trained, and this portion of the entertainment gives pronounced satisfaction The tableau" Greater Britain"is especially eff.?ctive. There is no lack of variety. Miss Onra gives a clever performance on the tight wire. and Victor Scoble, the quick change artiste, appears in a facial entertainment, assuming some diffinilt roles. Carona and Thomas are acccmplished acrobats, and Tom Gillerio.the Artiericui musical ckwn contributes a novel and laughter provoking item. Claude Oh my displays great ability as an equestrian in his jockey act and little lhly, the child rider, maintains her popularity. A buck jumping race which is taken part in by members of the audielce provides plenty of excitement. On Thursday eveniug,Claude Ohrny took a well deserved benefit when special features were introluced. The last performance of the season will take place tn-nicht (Saturday.)
