div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, JUNE 8, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, JUNE 8, 1900.
Church Parades.

On Sunday morning the Warrington battalion attended a regimental church parade, conducted by Colenel Ridgway in the absence, through indisposition, of the chaplain, the Rev. Canon Willis, of %Varrington, but the rev, gentleman is expeoted to be in camp on Sundae next and to preach to the men. The Celonel read the lessons, prayers and psalms. Church parades were held in connection with each battalion and were largely attended by visitors. The weather on Sunday was exceedingly hot, and quite a number of the men fainted and had to be carried from the' field be the am- bulance corps. A striking feature its connection wi'.ll the parade of theSt.Helens battalion was the large num- ber of men in the ranks wearing their ordinary clothes, one whole half-company hi ig thus conspicuous by the absence of the uniform. Ir. was explained that there was no time to serve out tho unit'orra to these recruits bolero th3y started, bet that the uliforms would b 3 suppi in camp A numbe: of Warrington men were also in civilian attire but tt.ey received their unitorin in camp. Excellent arrangements had been made for the comfert of the mee. Quarermester Pater is again to b 3 com- plimented upon so thoroughly carrying out all the &tails for which he is responsible. He has an able assistant in Q rartermaster Sergeant Willcock. The catering for the officers is being satisfactorily done ucder the super- intendence of Mrs. Barker and Mrs. Powis, while the sereeants, as usual., appointed a committee to look after their interests. with Colour-Sergeant Spencer as nve,s presideat, tati irterms.ster Bennion as treasurer, aril a?rgeant Pict as s ensstary. The men arc rectvin tne best attention so far as medical skill is concerned at the hands of Surgeon Captain Adams and Surgeon-Lieu- ten tnt Patterson, the former having lial the honour of being appointed the officer in charge of the brigade hospital. The health of the battalion has beea remark- ably good AO far, although the heat has at times leen very great. The non-commissioned officers, as usual,are displaying great efficiency. Sergeent-Alsjer R,awlinsoe is doing good work, and amongst others occupying their usual positions may ha mentioned Drill-Instructor Barker Arrneurer-Serp.,,eant Davies. and Quartermaster-S rgeant Bennie°, orderly room clerk.

div.head: LOCAL VOLUNTEERS UNDER CANVAS.
div.p: LOCAL VOLUNTEERS UNDER CANVAS.
A Pleasant Time at Conway.

A bright sun, a cloudless sky and a gentle sea breeze have been the pleasant conditions under which our citizsn soldiers have spent this week's encampment at Conway. This year the period of encampment has been extended to a fnrtnight, and if the present fine weather continues, the men will return with sun-burnt countenances and all the ap- pearances of well-seasone d soldiers. some time ago it appeared coubtful whether any Volunteer camp would be held at Conway this year, in conse- quence of the new movement for huge camps of instruction at Salisbury Plain and Aldershot. It was rumoured that the Warrington men would go to Altcar, but difficuties were encountered which could nnt be overcome, and it was ultimately de- cided that they should be included in a Lancashire brigade camp to be formed on the Alorfa at Conway where during the whole of last week fatigue parties from the Ist and 2nd V.B. South Lancashire Regiment and the let, 2nd,and 3rd Lancashire Fan- ners were busily engaged in preparing camps for the accommodation of the men of their respective battalions, with the result that a great part of the wide expanse of the Conway Mona is now covered with tents.

Conway is a favourite camping ground with the Warrington Volunteers and needless to say an effort was made by most of them to put in the full four- teen days' training. In this connection they were loyally supported by their employers who in the majority of eases willingly gave the ex- tended holiday. T,,i.4 spirit has been doubtless prompted by t ot the Warrington Volun teere in volue terHi o roailv for active service in South Mr.:A. he prn, yeir will live long in the antis o th,, Volunt-e o velment in the town as a most; iii",-norable one. It is unnecessary for us to recapitulate 01 ree•nt events in locAl volunteer circles in regard to the war in South Africa. Suffice it to say that; two contingents are now at the front, one consisting of 67 men under the command of Captain .M. App won, and the other of 20 men in charge of Lieutenant G. P. Carey. Both contin- gents consist of men of splendid physique and are in every way worthy representa- tives of the Warrington Volunteers. It is perhaps only natural that the patriotic spirit so manifest of late, should be reflected to some ex- tent in a large number of recruits joining the bat- talion. Never before has the local battalion shown such signs of vitality and strength, and this is largely due to the energetic efforts of Colonel Ridgway and Mejor Roome (the papular adjutant). Recruits have joined in scores and it is yet within ,the range of probability that the total strength will reach at least one thousand. Despite the fact dint there are nearly 90 men of the battalion in South Africa,the number in camp this year exceeds that of any previous encampment. No fewer than 672 Warringcon Velunteers are at Conway, namely 13 officers, 26 sergeants, 16 buglers, and 617 rank and tile. Colonel Ridgway is in command, and the other officers present are Major and Adjutant Roome Major Buck' on,Captains JO Fairclough,BFairclough J A Edelsteu (supply and transport officer of the brigade) Lieutenants Medley, Gough, Roberts and Williamson, Lieutenant and Quarter-master Potter, ~.3tirgeon• Captain Adams and surgeon-Lieutenant Patterson.

It may be said that the work of the camp this year will have less of a holiday character about it than prevbasly. First of all there will be a special course of musketry. There will oe exercise in the making of shelter trenches, and the attack and th- fence of positions, and in addition there will be battalion parades under regimental corn man ling officers. Generally speaking the work will be of ai practical a character as possible. Tnere will be but one ceremonial day—p irhaps not that,—but there will probably continually be some operations which will be interesting to the general public. There will be 1:13 sham fight actually concentrated on tee Morfa because of tee difficulty of manceuvring five regiments in a limited space, and especially Oa account of the musketry practice which will take place there. The year has also witnessed several important changes in the battalion. One of the most pleasing features is that Lieut.-Caloael Ridgway, who suc- ceeded the late Colonel J ,Greenell in the com- mand of the corps, has been promoted to the rank of Colonel, and be has also had the honour of receiv- ieg the Volunteer officers' decoration, which has been thoroughly well earned. Several Volunteers are also on active service in South Africa as mem- bers of the Warrington Breech of the St. John Am- bulance Association, and that is satisfactory to be able to note that several young men have taken up commissions during the year, and are manifesting considerable interest in their new duties. Attentian should also be called to the fact that during the same period Captain Hutchinson, who has also had the honour of receiving the' has severed hiA long and honourable connection with the batta- lion, a connection extending over 40 years. He was subsequently entertained to dinner by the officers and presented with a silver tea and coffee service. Major H. J. Widdows, an able efficer, has retired from the battalion, and another face -which will be much missed is that of Bandmaster Thomas
Armstrong, who has Atlvned his connection with the band after 18 years' service. No man could have taken more interest in his work,and he leaves the band in a high state of efficiency.
The Departure.

Rarely have such scenes of enthusiasm been wit- nessed on the departure of the volunteers from Warrington for their encampments as was the case on Saturday evening. The time fixed for the train to leave for Conway was nine o'clock, but long before that hour the streets presented quite an animated appearance. Everyone seemed bent on obtaining a view of the men as they marched to the station, and every coign of vantage was secured. Some of the more daring climbed to the top of the hoardings, and the crowd in the vicinity of the Park was very daw-e. The men after obtaining their rifles from the Drill Hall;paraded at eight o'clock on the lawn in front of the Town Hall: By this time the Town Hall steps, the balcony of the Conservative Club and the drives were crowded with sight seers. On the signal to start being given the regimental band, under the conductorship of the newly appointed bandraAiter, Mr J T Richardson, struck up the familiar strains of" The Old Folks at Horne," followed by " The girl I left behind me "and " We shall meet and we shall raisa him," The men experienced some difficulty owing to the crowded condition of Sankey- street and Parker-street in reaching the station. At several points en route cheers were raised and a casual observer would no doubt have thought that a "send-off" was being given to soldiers who were proceeding to South Africa inatead of to no more distant a place, than Conway. A large number of people managed to make their way on ta the plar,- form and the scene as the train steamed out of the tation at aboat 9 15 was one of- the greatest e n- thusiasm.

div.head: At Conway.
div.p: At Conway.

It was not until close on midnight when th men ar- rived in came. A little earlier a portinn of the cyclist company had arrived. Twenty of them travelled tn Conway on their machines—a distance from Warrington of abou's 70 miles—the route taken being through Mold. There were several punctures,which were soon rectifie.t. and,aided by the glorious weathnr, the riders succeeded in reachin7 camp at about eleven o'clock, having been en the road since half-pnst two in the afternoon. Lieutenant Gough was in command. The Warrineton battalion was the first to put in an appearanel at Con- way and is this matter th,y had been more fortqnato than their nomrades from Manchester and St. Hehnis in lying provided with tacilities for travelling on Saturday. The other bitt dims did not arrive until about noon on Sondaysthe traina following each other at shcr-, int '.ne,ls. They detrained at the Pentnaenta.ch siclinn, in close proxitrniy to the camp, marnhinn thence to their resner- tive quarters. The whole of the operations were carri,nl out without the slightest hitch or delay. The 2n.' , from St. Helens, name in two trains, at were under the corrmand of Colonel W. W. Pilkington, entering camp 892 strong. The Ist VII. Lancashire Fusiliers (Bury) also filled two train's, and marched into camp 680 strong out of a total of 930. This is the lareest contingent ever sent into camp from Bury. Thmv were under the command of Colonel T. Pilkingtnn Young. The 2nd Volunteer Battalion Lancashire Volunteers,unner the command of Colonel Phillips, nut 550 men undr..r canvas out of a total strength at 800 L entenamt Col Haworth brought in the strongest contingent of aid, his battalion, the 3rd Volunteer Battalon Lancashire Fusiliers (Salford), turning up 940 stronn, out of a total strength of 1,250. With !hir regiment was ire honorary colonel, Mr. L.r3 Knowles, M.P. The brigade is in command of Bri;adier General Loth Ross,in whose staff era inn'uded Cobol .I,n!el•rni as briende major, Captain E lelstrm as supply and transport officer, witn Setgmant Major G4llop,of Sal Carl. as hrign.de sergeant major, and Staff Sergeant Whit,fild, of St. Haernr, as brigade clerk.

div.head: Monday's Work.
div.p: Monday's Work.

Work commenced in real earnest on Meeday morning. All the battalions put in at least one drill comprising a number of evolutions, an inspection by the commend- in officer, and a march past. Two battalions, in feet, occepied the whole day working thus,namely those from St. Helens and Rochdale. Tee Warrington ani Bury contingents were else employed in &Ass firing on a range formed along the shore. Sixteen targets of the dummy p attern had been fired up and the ranges had been trk vt from 200 to 1000 yards. E Lei mseis to fire at least fifty rounds of ball ammunition, at the rate of 21 rounds e day. The ammunitioe is th et known pooularly as the Durn-Dam, and it is sugees..eri that the Govern- ment may be using it thus as they do not mean to e.npley i gain in warfare. The Salford men were employed ie the construction of shelter trenches on the 'and beaeh near Penmaenbach. The work done throuehout tete cern° was very satisfactory. In the early ev.rnine the camp presented an extremely busy appearance. In one spot heaps of clothing were laid out and surrounded ner men who were being served. Teem are special garments for rough work, to save the ordinary full-dress uniforms. The evening meal over and the washing, brushing, and polishing up cmpleted the volenteers who were riot on guard or fatigue duty, were allowed to go to Cenway, Dereanwy, or Penneaen- mawr, for amusement. Those desiring to go to Llandudno were accommodated with a speeial cheap train from the Penmaenbach siding,close to the camp.

div.head: Tuesday.—Pretoria Rejoicings.
div.p: Tuesday.—Pretoria Rejoicings.

The weather on Tuesday morning was by no means go delightful as us the preceding two days, a thick haze ob3curit g the horizon. Th-re was a slight fall of rain just before neon, hu., afterwards the weather brightened up, and a coel north-east wind sprang up. The Bury and Warrington regiments creeupied the ranges. Having cornpitted the 300 cards range on Mon- day they oe Tuesday fieished the 500 yards. Owing to ths difficulty of keeping the numer ms visi- tors to the Mona trom approaching too near the ranges, the danger signal; have been greatly extended and addi- tional precautions taken. This has been deemed neces- sary because the firing lines include many recruits who are unaccustomed to the prevalent conditions, have never before fired from the mar...eine rifles in rapid volleys, and have consequently displayed some amount of nervousness. Considering these facts, the firing is crn3ideted to have been fairly good. A portion of the St. Helens Battalion were taken out to the seashore near Penrnaenbach railway siding. and after receiving in- struction in entrenching work were put through prac- tical trench-making, similar to that which the Salford Battalion went through the day before. Toe Saltord and Rochdale Battalions and a portion of the Warrington Battalion had battalion parpes ueder their awn officers, working to instructioue from the Brigadier-General. No. 5 Company. Bury, did some interesting work as scouts. The old methods of instruc- tion have almost entirely disappeared, the revolution is complete, and the object is to give the men as cemplete , a training as possible during the fortnight which will be I spent here—a training which would render them useful in any emergency. A good deal of time was spent on Tuesday in signalling practice from the summit of the meuetains just outside the camp. At about 20 minutes past two o'clock a rumour spread , through the camp that Pretoria, had fallen. The news was received with the greatest enthusiasm, and the men wild with excitement, and headed by the band of the 2nd V.B South Lancashire Regiment, (St. Helens), marceed round the camp cheering vociferously, wevine Bags, and singing patriotic and loyal sons. Clvers were given for the Queen and groans for Kruger. Every flag that could be seized was taken from the linos anal utilised in the procession. A stoppaga was made at each , section of toe camp to play and sing the National Anthem, which was invariably followed by outbursts of cheering which could be heard at the extreme end of , Morfa. A holiday was given to the Salford men, althoueh the work for the day had all been mapped out I and lwas in progress. The firing operations, however. continued without intermission. At night hundreds of Volunteers assembled in Conway to witness the demons- tration promoted to signalise the occupation of Pretoria.

div.head: Wednesday.
div.p: Wednesday.

On Wednesday. the Bury and Warrington men corn pleted their musketry practice. and whilst the Sa!for.l and Rochdale men were engaged in battalion drills dr, St. flelevs men were trench making. The parade of the Salfords was witnessed by Colonel Ross, the Briga- dier, who also made a minute inspection of the men's evioment. The weather in the morning was very hot, hut in the afternoos there was a fresh breers hie winv. in from the sea. At half-past four the Salford men paraded for bathing.

Departure of the Lymm Volunteers The Lymm (ED Company of the 3r,i Vol. Batt. Cheshire Regiment loft Lymm about nine o'clock on Sunday morning for Timperley, under the carama,nd of Captain Groves and Lieutenant Ridgway. They were accompanied to the Eitation by the Lymm Church Band and a large number of interested L': mm residents. At Timper:ey they jlined the remaining companies ot ths battalion and proceeded to Salisbury Plain. where they arrived lat, in the evening. 'They will probably remain in camp a fortnight.

div.head: Runcorn Volunteers at Salisbury.
div.p: Runcorn Volunteers at Salisbury.

About 170 of Runcorn's Volunteer Corps in command of Captain Ashton, departed for Salisbury Plain on Saturday, joining the rest of the 2nd Volunteer Batt 'lion Cheshire Regiment at Belsby. The journey occupied from 2.30 p.m. to 1130 p.m. Provision had been ngisly made to satiefy the inner man en route, but at Salsbury Camp on Sunday there wis a great sra city o bread, which has been described as a " famine," and the Runcorn men had their share of th:s discunfort. War Office arrangements gone wrong again! On Monday the men succeeded to c,tamanloerin; boAl bread and biscuits and since thtt time the food has been plentiful. On Tuniday the 2nd Clies'eire had a long spell of outpost duty and on Wednesday one portion of the Ite,:iment was formed into a " convoy " and the remainder of the regiment, became an attecking force and the evolutions were very interesring, The Cheshire men are described as ;swing displayed the greatest eathusissin on the capture of Pretoria of any regiment in the camp.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
ALLEGED WOUNDING AT NEWTON

At the Warrington Occasional Court on Tuesday, before Mr. James Tinsley, Michael Mannion was brought up on a charge of wounding Patrick Delaney at Newton on the 40 of Jun.—Ouly suffi- cient evidence to justify a remand was offered and the hearing of the case was adjourned until Tues- day next. VIADUCT INSTITUTE BOWLING CLUB, EARLEiTOWN.

On Saturday in connection with this club, Mr. Beatty's annual prize of a guinea (a pair of bowls and jack) was bowled for on the club green. There were 37 entries, and the green being in splendid condition, there were some close finishes. in the end, Mr. S Thotnson g)t, th.i first prizi, Mr. F Mottram, 2nd and Mr J Boon_ 3rd. ST. PETER'S YOUNG MEN'S BIBLE CLASS, NEWTON.

gOn Saturday the members of the ablve class, to the number of abut 3i), in charge of the Rev. J. Ryder, vicar of St. Peter's Church, paid a visit to Owen's CoPege, Manchester, for the purpose of making an inspection of the pla,!e. An interesting feature of the visit was a lecture by the Rec. Mr. Boyd-Dawkins oa " England's history." The subject was incited in a very able manner, and the visitors were mucti edified.

div.head: Goon TEMPLARY.
div.p: Goon TEMPLARY.

The Hope )f Earbistown Lodge meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Wargrave-road, on Mon- day evening, Bro. Singleton presiding. Two friends were admitted to membership, Bro. Cux mins sent his resignation as marshal, as owing to his duties as a volunteer, he would be unable to attend. The resignation was, with regret accepted, and Bro. Sharp was appointed as marshal.—The Lodge was closed by Bro. Singleton, the remainder of the even- ing being spPnt in various games. WHIT MONDAY AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

By the various works at Earlestown, W hit lon- day was not ob4erved as a holiday, but t Newton, Messrs, McCorquodale sal (Jo's, place was closed. A large number of men. however, absented them- selves from work at Earlestown, the beautiful weather tempting the men away, All the shops in the town were closed, and the employees took ad- vantage of the holi,iay. The general holiday of the various works will take place in August; and this will account for Whit Monday being allowed to pass unnoticed. LIBERAL MEETING AT GOLBORNE.

A meeting was held at the Libel Ell Club, Golborne, on Thursday last week, for the purpose of electing the council and executive committee in connection with the Newton Division Liberal AsBo- - The chair was taken by Mr T and he was supported by Messrs H B Shores (Widnes), W Wiunard, R Openshaw, and others. An interesting lecture was given by Mr Aldrich, of Huyton, on " The Housing of the Poor." Votes of thanks accorded to the Chairman and Mr. Aldrich brought the proceedings to a close. DARING BURGLARY AT EARLESTOWN.

On Friday night three dwelling-houses in St. Helens-road, Newton Common, Earlestown, were burglariously entered, and articles of v due stolen therefrom. The houses are in the oc,Aipation of Messrs It Eaton, J Stacey. and 'Althorn, and were each properly secured befors the pople retired to rest at half past eleven. Next morning before six o'clock, they found that their houses had been entered. Examination showed that in each cas-.3 entry WR9 effected by the back windows, a hole being bored through the sash, and a piece of wire inserted and hooked on the catch which was then drawn back, and the window opened. At Mr Eaton's the thief or thieves actually entered the bed- room where he and his wife were sleeping and took from Mr. Eaton's trousers pocket a sovereign, and in the kitchen from a dresser about Sc was taken, a postal order being left. At Mr. Stacey's a gold ring and pocket handkerchief were stolen, and from Mr. Latham's, a silver watch from the bedroom, and a silver albert attached to a white metal watch, the latter being left. The matter was at once reported to the police, but at present there is no clue to the perpetrators of the thefts. It is not 12 months since the Co-operative Society's shop on the Common was broken into.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
A WOMAN'S ATTEMPTEu SUICIDE.

At St. Helens, on Tuesday, Jane Elalitwell, married woman, of Back 26, Ezokston-street, was charged on remand with atten.tated suicide. Mrs Halliwell, on May 28th, after her acc)nd husbaad had left ker, drank a quantity of laudanum. She had been remanded to Walton Gaol for eight days, and was now discharged on promising that she would not repeat the offence. DEATH OF AN OLD INHABITANT.

One of the oldest, inbabit•antsof St.:F.l4.mi, Mr Andrew Haw ksey, cabinet manufacturer, of Blldwin-street, died on Sunday at the advanced age of ninety-five. Mr. Hawkey has tmen in business considerably over sixty years, and was:regarded in Liverpool and by the timber trade generally 03 the greatest authority in the country on mahogany. He was in all timber disputes regarded as the final reference. Tux T. HELENS TRSJAWAY TRAFFIC.

The new Sc. Helens and District framvara.y Company have during the Whitsuntide horidays been exceptionally busy, the previous reword of number of passengers being more than doubled. The trams are now run by electricity instead of steam, and several extensions are runn•ng, notably, the Parr extension to Darhyshire Hill. In the three days—Saturda.y, Sunday, and Mroaday—the ears ran 5,204 mile 3, and 03,408 pasvngers were carried, agdiosc 1,540 mile last year, and JB,9l9_pvoeugers.

div.head: SERIOUS AFFAIEt AT A GLASS Vioaxs:
div.p: SERIOUS AFFAIEt AT A GLASS Vioaxs:

James Geer, a glass making apprentice employed bv Messrs. Thlkington Bros., was again brought before tie magistrates on Wednesday, on a charge of wounding George Dean, with intent to do him !grievous bodily harm. Chief Constable Wood said that Goer struck Dean on the head with a heavy iron Wow-pine in the works on Wednesday morning, the 30th ult. Dean was now under the d0c.,,.0r. A remand of one week had already expired. Mr. H. L. Riley,who appeared for the defence, said it wraill be convenient to all parties if a further remand of fourteen days was granted on the same bail—Ge • r in -5220 and two sureties of £lO each. The Bench agreed.

div.head: MILITARY NOTES.
div.p: MILITARY NOTES.

The 2nd Ra ttalion Royal Lancsshire 'Reserve Regi- ment is now lx-ing formed at Aldershot and all ex- soldiers who have been enli•ted at Warrington join thiA new battalion. Recruiting for the Royal Reserve Regiments ceased on Friday and no more offers of service are to be accepted.

Captain Nicholson late of the Liverpool Reg:ment who is now doing duty at the depot at Warrington, has beeii granted the temporary rank of Captain while temporarily employed at Warrington. The end of the South African Campaign now be- in,c,Y within sight the authorities are already consi- dering the matter of bringing home the large num- ber of militia units now serving there. Oce of the first to con home will be the 3rd battalion South Lancashire Regiment which was embodied at War- rington on the 13th of December last. Lieutenant Barker, late of 6th battalion Kings Liverpol Regiment with headquarters at Warring- ton, haying rejoined the militia has been appointed Captain in the battalion. _ _ _ _ _

_ .Major Willis, who lately retired from the 4th battalion Cheshire Reginaent on that corps going to South Africa ha; been appointed Captain in the South Earl of Scotland Militia Artillery with the rank of Major in the Militia force. Second Lieut Gape, ot !;he 5!.,e battalion Liver- pool Regiment with headquarters at Warrington has ben appointed to a commission in the regular service, joining the new 3rd battalion Liverpool Regiment. :Seceni Lieut Hall of the old Ist Ches- hire militia has also been appointed to a eommii- sion in the Liverpool Regiment.whik Second Lieut. Rowland Hill also appointed to a commission in the regular service becomes an officer of the 2ad battalion Cheshire Regiment in South Africa with which corps he has. been serving as an attached militia officer. Surgeon Captain King,M.D., of the 2nd Volunteer Battalion Cheshire Regiment, having been formally appointed senior medical officer of the Cheshire Volunteer Infantry Brigade, has been promoted to the rank of Brigade Surgeon Lieutenant Colonel. He has been jest over eleven years in the service. Major Garnon becomes seconi in command of the 2nd Volunteer Battalion Cheshire Regiment in place of Major Yerburei, Woo has left the ser- vice after being an officer of the corps only since July 1895 whem he was given a direct commission as major in the battalion.

div.head: DEAI H AND FUNERAL OF MISS COLE BURN.
div.p: DEAI H AND FUNERAL OF MISS COLE BURN.

It is with regret we record the death of Miss Coleburn, Odes% daughter of the laee Mr. Henry Coleburn, who for 45 years was registrar of births, deaths, and marriages for Runcorn and district. Misa Celeburn, who resided with her sister, Mrs. Waterworth, at the Egerton Arms Hotel, caught a chill while takine oart in the Queen's birthday celebration at Runcorn Town Hall on the night of the 24th ult. Pneu—onia followed, and although all that medical skill could suggest was done she succumbed on Thursday flightiest. For many years Miss Coleburn had been a most active worker in connection with Holy. Trinity Church and Schools, and her death has left a blank it will be somewhat difficult to fill. She was a teacher in the Sunday school, superintendent and treasurer of the Mother' Meeting, leader of the Scripture Union and Band of Hope, and a district visitor. The high regard and respect in which she was held was de- monstrated on Sunday afternoon, when her mortal re- mains were committed to their last resting place in Runcorn Cemetery. The choir boys of Holy Trinity, attired in their surplices, headed the mournful procession, and there were also present the members of the deceased lady's Sunday school clasc, the members of the Mothers' Meeting, and many others. A number of the male teachers officiated as bearers, al d walked beside the hearse,which was followed by four coaches. In the first at ere Mr and Mrs Cockerlyne. Mr E Cockerlyne, Mrs Blakemore, and Mrs Waterworth ; second coach, Mrs Coleburn, Miss Blakemore, the Misses Cockerlyne, and Mr Harry Water- worth; third coach, Mrs Mottram, Mrs Woodhouse. Mrs Elankinson, and Mrs Grirnwood ; fourth coach, Mr H Flankinson, Mr C J Cunningham, aad Miss Tyrie. A fifth coach, containing Rev C 11 Killick and the Rev N J Poole, preceded the hearse. The first put of the service was nerf irineel in Holy Trinity Church, by the Wv C R Killick, and the hymn "Peace, perfect paics " was impressively rendered by the choir and congregation. Mr Cockerlyne, brother-in-law of the deceased lady, presided at the creep, anti as the cortege left the church, he played the "Dead March." At tee grave side Mr. Killick and Mr. Poole taok part in the eervice, and the chair boys sang "Jean, Lover of my soul," Floral tributes were sent by the following : Mrs Waterworth and chi'dren, sisters and Deices, and Mrs Coleburn, Rev and Mrs Killick, Rev N J Poole, Teachers of Holy Trinity Sunday School, Mothers' Meet- ing (two), Sunday School Class, Band of Hop e, Miss Henderson, Mr Mettram, Mrs Grirriwoed, Mrs Dunn,Mr and Mrs Fred Seddoe (Southport), Ms i Jonas, and Mr E Turner. Oar Sunday night, at Trinity Church, the Rev NJ Poole preached a funeral mermen, in which he paid a glowiug tribute to the high character and vein- able work of Miss Coleburn.

div.head: 110 MILES AN HOUR.
div.p: 110 MILES AN HOUR.
The Proposed Mono-Railway. Power Station at Warringt on.

"For some time past," says " Feilden'e Magazine," "there has been an increasing dsmand for more rapid means of transit between Mauclaester and Liverpool.but the practical limit of speed upon ordinary railroads has already been attained. It is now proposed to make use of the angle rail system invented lw Mr. Behr, by tbe aid of which a speed of 110 miles an hour may safely be employed, thus reducing the dura- then of the journey to about 20 minutes. The construc- tion of the Behr mono-rail system is exceedinely A single rail is fixed on the top ef steel trestle supports 4ft high, on which the car is supported, and balanced, whilst guide rails are provided on the lower part of the trestles to take internal pressure when curves are being parsed. The car is con- structed with longitudinal Keats placed back to back, and the rail occupies spec between the two seats. Therefore a considerable proportion of the weight is below the line of support. and as the electric motors are also carried in the lower portion of the car, the centre of gravity is sa low that derailment should be practically impossible. In the present example it is proposed that a central power station shalt be established at Warring- ton whence eleatricity will be carried along the line by conduits to transformers from which it will pass along the guide-rails to the motors beneaeh the car. An automatic arrangement provides for the safety of each car, and as there are no intermediate stations, management of the traffic will present none of the difficulttes experienced on ordinary railways Satisfactory trials of the Behr system have already been made in Ireland and Beleium, end a committee of inves- tigation appointed by the Liverpool Chainter of Com- merce reported so favuurably upon the matter that the present cempany has been termed, with a capital of £2,000,000, to undertake the censtruction of the Tee eelv thing now wanted is the appeoval of Parliament. Of course there is opposition, but this is eentlaed to three railway companies who di like competition and t) some local autherities who will receive no direct b heefit And possibly desire that otticr people should have eone. The Corporation of Salford in particular, aje.cts to the new lint, on mithetic grounds, believing it will seriously dis- figure the town, wtost heauties are no doubt familiar to mot of our readere. Expert evideune tendered Mere the Parliamentary Cenamitcee, under the presidency of Sir John Benna.way,is en.irely favourable to the sceetne to which we wish every success."
